## Appendix A Preliminaries

We review the lifted product (LP) code construction [54, 41]. We begin with hypergraph product (HGP) codes [38] and then show that the lifted product is a natural generalization of the HGP construction obtained by replacing scalar binary matrices with matrices whose entries lie in a group ring. We then recast both constructions from the perspective of homological algebra, where hypergraph product and lifted product codes can be described as tensor product chain complexes and their logical operators associated with the homology of the chain complex. Throughout, we are interested in error-correcting codes on qubits and hence always work over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ .

### A Hypergraph product codes

A classical linear code over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ can be defined by a parity-check matrix $H\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r\times c}$ , where $c$ is the number of bits and $r$ is the number of parity checks. The codewords are precisely the vectors in $\ker H$ . A CSS code can be specified by two parity-check matrices $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ that satisfy the commutation condition $H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0$ . The hypergraph product code construction gives a systematic way to construct such pairs of parity-check matrices from two classical codes.

#### Definition 5 (Hypergraph product code).

Let $A\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ and $B\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}$ . The hypergraph product (HGP) code [38] associated with $(A,B)$ is the CSS code on $n=c_{1}c_{2}+r_{1}r_{2}$ physical qubits with parity-check matrices

$$ \displaystyle H_{X} \displaystyle=\bigl[A\otimes I_{c_{2}}\;\big|\;I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{T}\bigr], \displaystyle H_{Z} \displaystyle=\bigl[I_{c_{1}}\otimes B\;\big|\;A^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}}\bigr]. $$

This definition ensures that the CSS commutation condition holds:

$$ \displaystyle H_{X}H_{Z}^{T} \displaystyle=(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B)^{T}+(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{T})(A^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}})^{T} \displaystyle=A\otimes B^{T}+A\otimes B^{T} \displaystyle=0. $$

where the last equality follows since we are working over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ .

#### Definition 6 (Kernel dimensions).

For a binary matrix $M$ , define

$$ h(M)=\dim\ker M,\qquad h^{\perp}(M)=\dim\ker M^{T}. $$

The hypergraph product code has

$$ k=h(A)h(B)+h^{\perp}(A)h^{\perp}(B) $$

logical qubits. If $A$ and $B$ are full-row-rank parity-check matrices for classical codes of dimensions $h(A)$ and $h(B)$ , then $h^{\perp}(A)=h^{\perp}(B)=0$ and the formula reduces to $k=h(A)h(B)$ . We can also obtain a simple lower bound on $k$ in terms of the dimensions of $A$ and $B$ assuming they have more columns than rows:

$$ k\geq(c_{a}-r_{a})(c_{b}-r_{b}). $$

#### Example 1.

The unrotated surface code is an example of a hypergraph product between two repetition codes.

Let $\operatorname{Rep}(d)$ denote the length- $d$ repetition code with parity-check matrix

$$ H_{\mathrm{rep}}(d)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0&\cdots&0\\
0&1&1&\ddots&\vdots\\
\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\
0&\cdots&0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{(d-1)\times d}. $$

Taking $A=B=H_{\mathrm{rep}}(d)$ in the hypergraph product construction gives the distance- $d$ unrotated surface code with parameters $\llbracket d^{2}+(d-1)^{2},\,1,\,d\rrbracket.$

LP codes generalize HGP codes by replacing binary matrix entries with elements of a group algebra. Thus, before introducing lifted product codes, we first fix some group conventions we use to describe our code families, and then review the group theory background needed for the construction.

### B Group conventions and group algebras

Many of the groups used in our code constructions can be written as direct products or semidirect products. As the definition for a direct product is unambiguous, we just specify the convention used for semidirect product.

#### Definition 7 (Semidirect product).

Let $N$ and $H$ be two groups, let $\varphi:H\to\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ be a group homomorphism, where $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ denotes the group of automorphisms of $N$ under composition, and let $\varphi_{h}=\varphi(h)$ . Then, the semidirect product $N\rtimes_{\varphi}H$ is defined as the set of pairs $(n,h)\in N\times H$ with multiplication

$$ (n,h)\cdot(n^{\prime},h^{\prime})=\left(n\varphi_{h}(n^{\prime}),hh^{\prime}\right)\qquad\forall n,n^{\prime}\in N,\quad h,h^{\prime}\in H. $$

We abbreviate $(n,e_{H})$ by $n$ and $(e_{N},h)$ by $h$ . Then $nh=(n,h)$ , so every element is written uniquely with its $N$ -factor first. Written with this convention, a direct calculation with the multiplication law Eq. 13 gives

$$ hn=(e_{N},h)(n,e_{H})=(\varphi_{h}(n),h)=\varphi_{h}(n)h, $$

or equivalently,

$$ \varphi_{h}(n)=hnh^{-1}. $$

As the lifted product construction applies to any finite group $G$ , we next review the necessary background on group algebras and their representations.

#### Definition 8 (Group ring and regular representations).

Let $G$ be a finite group. The group algebra

$$ \mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]=\left\{\sum_{g\in G}\alpha_{g}g\;:\;\alpha_{g}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}\right\} $$

is the $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -vector space with basis $G$ and multiplication induced by the group law. We write $\mathtt{b}(g)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|}$ for the standard basis vector corresponding to $g\in G$ . By linearity, a ring element $a=\sum_{g}\alpha_{g}g\in\mathcal{R}$ corresponds to the binary vector

$$ \mathtt{b}(a)=\sum_{g\in G}\alpha_{g}\mathtt{b}(g). $$

The left regular representation and right regular representation are first defined on group elements by

$$ L(g)\mathtt{b}(h)=\mathtt{b}(gh),\qquad R(g)\mathtt{b}(h)=\mathtt{b}(hg^{-1}),\qquad g,h\in G, $$

and then extended linearly to all $a\in\mathcal{R}$ . When the context is clear, we suppress the $\mathtt{b}(\cdot)$ notation and write, for example, $R(g)h=hg^{-1}$ , meaning $R(g)\mathtt{b}(h)=\mathtt{b}(hg^{-1})$ . In coordinates, for $a=\sum_{g}\alpha_{g}g$ , these matrices are

$$ L(a)_{y,x}=\alpha_{yx^{-1}},\qquad R(a)_{y,x}=\alpha_{y^{-1}x},\qquad x,y\in G. $$

The left and right regular representations commute:

$$ L(a)R(b)=R(b)L(a)\qquad\forall\,a,b\in\mathcal{R}. $$

When we have a matrix $M$ defined over $\mathcal{R}$ , we can expand it to a binary matrix by replacing each entry with its corresponding left or right regular representation. We will overload notation and denote the binary matrix obtained by replacing each entry of $M$ with its left (resp. right) regular representation as $L(M)$ (resp. $R(M)$ ). Similarly, if we have a vector $v$ where each entry is a ring element, we write $\mathtt{b}(v)$ for the binary vector obtained by replacing each entry of $v$ with its corresponding binary vector.

#### Definition 9 (Involution and conjugate transpose).

For $a=\sum_{g}\alpha_{g}g\in\mathcal{R}$ , its involution is defined as

$$ a^{*}=\sum_{g\in G}\alpha_{g}g^{-1}. $$

For a matrix $M$ over $\mathcal{R}$ , its conjugate transpose $M^{*}$ is defined entrywise as

$$ (M^{*})_{ij}=(M_{ji})^{*}. $$

This definition of conjugate transpose over the ring is compatible with the ordinary binary transpose after expansion:

$$ L(M^{*})=L(M)^{T}\quad\text{and}\quad R(M^{*})=R(M)^{T}. $$

To see this, first take a single group element $g\in G$ . The matrices $L(g)$ and $R(g)$ are permutation matrices, and transposing a permutation matrix gives the inverse permutation. Hence $L(g)^{T}=L(g^{-1})$ and $R(g)^{T}=R(g^{-1})$ . Extending linearly gives, for $a=\sum_{g}\alpha_{g}g$ ,

$$ L(a)^{T}=\sum_{g}\alpha_{g}L(g)^{T}=\sum_{g}\alpha_{g}L(g^{-1})=L(a^{*}), $$

and the same argument applies to $R(\cdot)$ . For matrices over $\mathcal{R}$ , the ordinary binary transpose also swaps block positions, which is exactly the swap in $(M^{*})_{ij}=(M_{ji})^{*}$ .

We now have all the necessary tools to define the lifted product code construction.

### C Lifted product codes

Lifted product codes generalize hypergraph product codes through a richer internal structure afforded by the regular representations of a group algebra. Instead of taking the product of two ordinary binary classical codes, we allow the parity-check matrices to have entries in a group algebra, and each group algebra entry expands to a structured binary block via its left and right regular representations. The left and right regular representations are the two commuting actions that make this expansion compatible with the CSS commutation condition.

#### Definition 10 (Lifted product code).

Let $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ for a finite group $G$ , and let $A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ and $B\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}$ . The lifted product code $\textrm{LP}(A,B)$ is the CSS code on $n=|G|\,(c_{1}c_{2}+r_{1}r_{2})$ physical qubits with parity-check matrices given by

$$ \displaystyle H_{X} \displaystyle=\bigl[L(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})\;\big|\;R(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{*})\bigr], \displaystyle H_{Z} \displaystyle=\bigl[R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B)\;\big|\;L(A^{*}\otimes I_{r_{2}})\bigr]. $$

The lifted product construction can be viewed as a generalization of the hypergraph product construction (5)–(6) where the tensor products and transposes are interpreted over the group algebra $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ and then expanded to binary matrices using the regular representations of $\mathcal{R}$ . We can verify that the CSS commutation condition holds for LP codes.

#### Remark 1 (Relation to balanced product codes).

Lifted product codes are a special case of the balanced product construction of [41]. The tensor product over $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ in (53) is the balanced product of two classical chain complexes, in which the diagonal action of $G$ is quotiented out via the balancing relation. When the chain groups are free modules, as in this case, the balanced and lifted products coincide.

#### Proposition 1 (CSS condition for LP codes).

The parity-check matrices $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ defined in (23)–(24) satisfy

$$ H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0. $$

#### Proof.

From Definition 10, we have

$$ H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=L(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})\,R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B)^{T}\;+\;R(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{*})\,L(A^{*}\otimes I_{r_{2}})^{T}. $$

Using the identities

$$ L(M)^{T}=L(M^{*}),\qquad R(M)^{T}=R(M^{*}) $$

followed by the identities

$$ (M\otimes I)^{*}=M^{*}\otimes I,\qquad(I\otimes N)^{*}=I\otimes N^{*}, $$

(25) simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle H_{X}H_{Z}^{T} \displaystyle=\underbrace{L(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})\,R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B^{*})}_{\displaystyle T_{1}}\;+\;\underbrace{R(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{*})\,L(A\otimes I_{r_{2}})}_{\displaystyle T_{2}} \displaystyle=0 $$

where we have obtained the last equality by using the identity $(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=AC\otimes BD$ and the fact that the left and right regular representations commute to show that $T_{1}=T_{2}$ and hence $T_{1}+T_{2}=0$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ .

∎

The number of physical qubits in the lifted product code is

$$ n=|G|\,(c_{1}c_{2}+r_{1}r_{2}), $$

since the two qubit blocks have sizes $c_{1}c_{2}$ and $r_{1}r_{2}$ over the group algebra, and each group-ring coordinate expands to $|G|$ binary coordinates. The number of logical qubits can always be computed from the expanded binary check matrices as

$$ k=n-\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}(H_{X})-\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}(H_{Z}) $$

which leads to the elementary lower bound

$$ k\geq|G|\bigl(c_{1}c_{2}+r_{1}r_{2}-r_{1}c_{2}-c_{1}r_{2}\bigr)=|G|\,(c_{1}-r_{1})(c_{2}-r_{2}). $$

In later sections when we prove distance bounds and construct a canonical logical basis for lifted product codes, it will be convenient to have a dictionary that lets us translate between working over the ring $\mathcal{R}$ and working over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ . We first fix our conventions. Over $\mathcal{R}$ , a matrix acts on column vectors from the left, as in $Mu$ , and on row vectors from the right, as in $vM$ ; matrix products over $\mathcal{R}$ multiply entries in the order written and are associative. In binary coordinates, we will always treat $\mathtt{b}(v)$ as a column vector, regardless of whether $v$ is a row or a column over $\mathcal{R}.$

Furthermore, because the blocks of the parity-check matrices in Definition 10 are Kronecker products over $\mathcal{R}$ , the vectors they act on are naturally indexed by pairs, and it will be convenient to view them as flattened matrices over $\mathcal{R}$ . For $V\in\mathcal{R}^{m\times m^{\prime}}$ , let $\operatorname{vec}(V)\in\mathcal{R}^{mm^{\prime}}$ denote the row-major flattening of $V$ , which lists the entries of the first row, then those of the second row, and so on:

$$ {\operatorname{vec}(V)}_{(i-1)m^{\prime}+j}=V_{ij},\qquad i\in\{1,\dots,m\},\quad j\in\{1,\dots,m^{\prime}\}. $$

The following proposition collects all the compatibility properties between the ring and binary descriptions that we will need.

#### Proposition 2.

Let $M\in\mathcal{R}^{r\times c}$ and $N\in\mathcal{R}^{r^{\prime}\times c^{\prime}}$ be matrices over $\mathcal{R}$ . The map $\mathtt{b}:\mathcal{R}^{c}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{c|G|}$ is a bijection that satisfies the following properties:

- (i) (Matrix-vector products) For a column vector $u\in\mathcal{R}^{c}$ and a row vector $v\in\mathcal{R}^{1\times c}$ ,

$$ L(M)\,\mathtt{b}(u)=\mathtt{b}(Mu)\quad\text{and}\quad R(M)\,\mathtt{b}(v)=\mathtt{b}(vM^{*}). $$

(32)

- (ii) (Kronecker products with an identity factor) For $V\in\mathcal{R}^{c\times m}$ and $W\in\mathcal{R}^{m\times c^{\prime}}$ ,

$$ L(M\otimes I_{m})\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V))=\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(MV))\quad\text{and}\quad R(I_{m}\otimes N)\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(W))=\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(WN^{*})). $$

(33)

#### Proof.

Using Definitions 8 and 9, it is straightforward to verify that $\mathtt{b}$ is a bijection that satisfies the stated properties. ∎

### D Mitten codes and structured mitten codes

In Definition 4, we defined mitten codes, which are a class of $\operatorname{LP}$ codes with $1\times 2$ base matrices and non-abelian $G$ with further condition that $L(a_{1})$ and $R(b_{1})$ being full-rank. Here we single out a structured subfamily whose extra algebraic symmetry lets the syndrome-extraction (SE) cycle run ideally twice as fast with 2 AODs (Appendix H.E). Recall the involution $a^{*}=\sum_{g}\alpha_{g}g^{-1}$ of Definition 8. A ring element is self-adjoint if $a^{*}=a$ . The structured mitten codes are mitten codes in which every base matrix entry is self-adjoint,

$$ a_{0}^{*}=a_{0},\quad a_{1}^{*}=a_{1},\quad b_{0}^{*}=b_{0},\quad b_{1}^{*}=b_{1}. $$

For specific parameters of both mitten and structured mitten codes studied in this paper, see Appendix K and Table 13.

### E Homological algebra

We will reformulate the lifted product construction in the language of homological algebra. This way of constructing lifted product codes is akin to the machinery of the more general balanced product construction of Ref. [41]. This perspective provides a systematic route to construct quantum codes from classical codes via tensor products of chain complexes and will later allow us to better understand the structure of the lifted product codes.

The starting observation is to note that a classical linear code can be described in terms of the homology of a two-term chain complex:

$$ C_{\bullet}:\quad C_{1}\xrightarrow{\partial=H}C_{0}, $$

where $C_{1}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{c}$ is the vector space of bits, $C_{0}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ is the vector space of parity checks, and the boundary map $\partial:C_{1}\to C_{0}$ is given by matrix multiplication by the parity-check matrix $H\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r\times c}$ . The classical linear code with parity-check matrix $H$ is precisely the first homology group $H_{1}(\mathcal{C}(\partial))=\ker\partial=\ker H$ , i.e. the set of vectors that satisfy all parity checks. The zeroth homology group $H_{0}(\mathcal{C}(\partial))=C_{0}/\im\partial=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}/\im H$ is nontrivial whenever the parity check matrix $H$ has linearly dependent rows.

One can view a CSS code as two separate classical codes with parity-check matrices $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ that must be compatible in the sense that they satisfy $H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0$ . The natural algebraic object that captures this compatibility is a three-term chain complex

$$ C_{2}\xrightarrow{\partial_{2}=H_{Z}^{T}}C_{1}\xrightarrow{\partial_{1}=H_{X}}C_{0} $$

where $C_{2}$ , $C_{1}$ , and $C_{0}$ are $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -vector spaces whose basis elements label the $Z$ checks, qubits, and $X$ checks respectively. Qubits are placed on $C_{1}$ , and the parity-check matrices are $H_{X}=\partial_{1}$ and $H_{Z}=\partial_{2}^{T}$ . The CSS commutation condition $H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0$ is then simply the statement that $\partial_{1}\partial_{2}=0$ , i.e. that (36) is indeed a chain complex. X-stabilizers are rows of $\partial_{1}$ , while Z-stabilizers are columns of $\partial_{2}$ (equivalently, rows of $\partial_{2}^{T}$ ). A Z-type logical operator commutes with all the $X$ -stabilizers but is not itself a $Z$ -stabilizer. Such an operator can be represented as a vector $z\in C_{1}$ that is in the kernel of $\partial_{1}=H_{X}$ but is not in the image of $\partial_{2}=H_{Z}^{T}$ . Hence Z-type logical operators are represented by nontrivial classes in the first homology group

$$ H_{1}=\ker\partial_{1}/\im\partial_{2}. $$

Dually, X-type logical operators are represented by the first cohomology group $H^{1}=\ker\partial_{2}^{T}/\im\partial_{1}^{T}$ .

The question, then, is how to produce a three-term chain complex that corresponds to a CSS code from classical input data in the form of two-term chain complexes. There is a standard algebraic construction that does exactly this: the tensor product of chain complexes.

#### Definition 11 (Tensor product of chain complexes).

Given two two-term chain complexes over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -valued vector spaces,

$$ C_{\bullet}^{A}:\;C_{1}^{A}\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{A}\;}C_{0}^{A},\qquad C_{\bullet}^{B}:\;C_{1}^{B}\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{B}\;}C_{0}^{B}, $$

their tensor-product complex $C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes C_{\bullet}^{B}$ is the three-term complex

$$ C_{1}^{A}\otimes C_{1}^{B}\;\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{2}\;}\;\bigl(C_{1}^{A}\otimes C_{0}^{B}\bigr)\oplus\bigl(C_{0}^{A}\otimes C_{1}^{B}\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{1}\;}\;C_{0}^{A}\otimes C_{0}^{B}, $$

with boundary maps

$$ \partial_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}I\otimes\partial_{B}\\
\partial_{A}\otimes I\end{bmatrix},\qquad\partial_{1}=\bigl[\,\partial_{A}\otimes I\;\big|\;I\otimes\partial_{B}\,\bigr]. $$

One can verify directly that $\partial_{1}\partial_{2}=0$ :

$$ \partial_{1}\partial_{2}=(\partial_{A}\otimes I)(I\otimes\partial_{B})+(I\otimes\partial_{B})(\partial_{A}\otimes I)=\partial_{A}\otimes\partial_{B}+\partial_{A}\otimes\partial_{B}=0, $$

so the tensor-product complex is indeed a chain complex, and the resulting CSS code automatically satisfies the commutation condition. To construct the hypergraph product code from classical codes with parity-check matrices $A$ and $B$ , we take the tensor product of the chain complex $C_{\bullet}^{A}$ with the dual of $C_{\bullet}^{B}$ .

#### Definition 12 (Dual of a chain complex).

Let $C_{\bullet}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{c}\xrightarrow{\;H\;}\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ be a two-term chain complex, where the chain groups are equipped with their standard bases. We define its dual complex as

$$ \hat{C}_{\bullet}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}\xrightarrow{\;H^{T}\;}\mathbb{F}_{2}^{c}. $$

The tensor product $C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}$ then has middle chain group $(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{c_{1}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{c_{2}})\oplus(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{1}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{2}})$ , and the maps $\partial_{1}$ and $\partial_{2}^{T}$ reproduce (5)–(6). The dimension of the code follows from the Künneth theorem.

#### Theorem 3 (Künneth formula [108]).

Let $C_{\bullet}$ and $D_{\bullet}$ be chain complexes of finite-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -vector spaces. Then the homology of their tensor product satisfies

$$ H_{n}(C_{\bullet}\otimes D_{\bullet})\cong\bigoplus_{i+j=n}H_{i}(C_{\bullet})\otimes H_{j}(D_{\bullet}). $$

For the hypergraph product, we apply this theorem to $C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}$ . Since the logical qubits are represented by the middle homology group, we obtain

$$ H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})\cong\bigl(H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})\otimes H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})\bigr)\oplus\bigl(H_{0}(C_{\bullet}^{A})\otimes H_{1}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})\bigr). $$

Taking dimensions gives the usual formula

$$ k=h(A)h(B)+h^{\perp}(A)h^{\perp}(B), $$

where

$$ h(A)=\dim\ker A,\qquad h^{\perp}(A)=\dim\ker A^{T}, $$

and similarly for $B$ .

To pass from the hypergraph product to the lifted product, we replace $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -vector spaces by modules over the ring $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ . A module can be thought of as generalizing the notion of a vector space by allowing scalars to come from a ring instead of a field.

#### Definition 13 ( $\mathcal{R}$ -modules).

Let $\mathcal{R}$ be a ring. A left $\mathcal{R}$ -module is an abelian group $M$ equipped with a scalar multiplication

$$ \mathcal{R}\times M\to M,\qquad(a,m)\mapsto am, $$

satisfying the following axioms for all $a,b\in\mathcal{R}$ and all $m,n\in M$ :

$$ \displaystyle a(m+n) \displaystyle=am+an, \displaystyle(a+b)m \displaystyle=am+bm, \displaystyle(ab)m \displaystyle=a(bm), \displaystyle 1m \displaystyle=m. $$

A right $\mathcal{R}$ -module is defined similarly, except that scalar multiplication acts on the right:

$$ M\times\mathcal{R}\to M,\qquad(m,a)\mapsto ma. $$

The corresponding axioms are

$$ \displaystyle(m+n)a \displaystyle=ma+na, \displaystyle m(a+b) \displaystyle=ma+mb, \displaystyle(ma)b \displaystyle=m(ab), \displaystyle m1 \displaystyle=m. $$

When $\mathcal{R}$ is commutative, left and right $\mathcal{R}$ -modules are equivalent.

#### Remark 2.

The distinction between left and right modules is not really about which side of $m$ we write the scalar. We could just as easily write a right action on the left, as $(a,m)\mapsto am$ , and define the associativity axiom by $(ab)m=b(am)$ instead of $(ab)m=a(bm)$ . This difference in the associativity axiom is the only true distinguishing feature between left and right modules.

#### Example 2.

The basic example is the free module $\mathcal{R}^{n}$ . Its elements are vectors

$$ v=\begin{pmatrix}r_{1}\\
\vdots\\
r_{n}\end{pmatrix},\qquad r_{i}\in\mathcal{R}. $$

When $\mathcal{R}^{n}$ is regarded as a left $\mathcal{R}$ -module, we use the notation ${}_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{n}$ and scalars $a\in\mathcal{R}$ act entrywise on the left:

$$ av=\begin{pmatrix}ar_{1}\\
\vdots\\
ar_{n}\end{pmatrix}. $$

When $\mathcal{R}^{n}$ is regarded as a right $\mathcal{R}$ -module, we use the notation $\mathcal{R}^{n}_{\mathcal{R}}$ and scalars $a\in\mathcal{R}$ act entrywise on the right:

$$ va=\begin{pmatrix}r_{1}a\\
\vdots\\
r_{n}a\end{pmatrix}. $$

Sometimes it will also be convenient for us to view the elements of ${}_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{n}$ as row vectors.

We constructed the hypergraph product code by taking the tensor product of two chain complexes defined over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -vector spaces. This was defined degree-by-degree from tensor products of the underlying vector spaces, as in (39). For lifted product codes, we use the same product-complex construction, but with vector spaces replaced by modules over the group algebra $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ .

To do this, we need the tensor product of modules over $\mathcal{R}$ . Let $K$ be a right $\mathcal{R}$ -module and let $L$ be a left $\mathcal{R}$ -module. Tensoring over $\mathcal{R}$ means that scalars from $\mathcal{R}$ should act as scalars in the combined object, rather than as data belonging separately to one factor or the other. Therefore, for $k\in K$ , $\ell\in L$ , and $a\in\mathcal{R}$ , multiplying $k$ by $a$ on the right should be identified with multiplying $\ell$ by $a$ on the left. This is enforced by the balancing relation

$$ (ka)\otimes\ell=k\otimes(a\ell). $$

This relation is the module analogue of the scalar-linearity relation in the tensor product of vector spaces that lets us move scalars across the tensor product. It only makes sense when the first module has a right $\mathcal{R}$ -action and the second module has a left $\mathcal{R}$ -action.

#### Definition 14 (Tensor product of $\mathcal{R}$ -modules).

Let $K$ be a right $\mathcal{R}$ -module and let $L$ be a left $\mathcal{R}$ -module. The tensor product $K\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L$ is the abelian group generated by formal symbols

$$ k\otimes\ell,\qquad k\in K,\ \ell\in L, $$

subject to the relations

$$ \displaystyle(k+k^{\prime})\otimes\ell \displaystyle=k\otimes\ell+k^{\prime}\otimes\ell, \displaystyle k\otimes(\ell+\ell^{\prime}) \displaystyle=k\otimes\ell+k\otimes\ell^{\prime}, \displaystyle(ka)\otimes\ell \displaystyle=k\otimes(a\ell), $$

for all $k,k^{\prime}\in K$ , $\ell,\ell^{\prime}\in L$ , and $a\in\mathcal{R}$ . The symbols $k\otimes\ell$ are called pure tensors and are said to generate $K\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L$ since any element of $K\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L$ can be written as a finite sum of pure tensors.

Just as the tensor product is only well-defined between a right module and a left module, the tensor product of chain complexes is only well-defined between a complex of right modules and a complex of left modules.

#### Definition 15 (Tensor product of a right-module complex and a left-module complex).

Let

$$ K_{\bullet}=\left(\cdots\longrightarrow K_{p+1}\xrightarrow{\partial^{K}_{p+1}}K_{p}\xrightarrow{\partial^{K}_{p}}K_{p-1}\longrightarrow\cdots\right) $$

be a chain complex of right $\mathcal{R}$ -modules, and let

$$ L_{\bullet}=\left(\cdots\longrightarrow L_{q+1}\xrightarrow{\partial^{L}_{q+1}}L_{q}\xrightarrow{\partial^{L}_{q}}L_{q-1}\longrightarrow\cdots\right) $$

be a chain complex of left $\mathcal{R}$ -modules. Their tensor product over $\mathcal{R}$ is the chain complex of abelian groups

$$ K_{\bullet}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L_{\bullet} $$

whose degree- $n$ term is

$$ \left(K_{\bullet}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L_{\bullet}\right)_{n}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}K_{p}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L_{q}. $$

The boundary map

$$ \partial_{n}:\left(K_{\bullet}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L_{\bullet}\right)_{n}\longrightarrow\left(K_{\bullet}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}L_{\bullet}\right)_{n-1} $$

is defined on pure tensors by

$$ \partial_{n}(k\otimes\ell)=\partial^{K}_{p}(k)\otimes\ell+(-1)^{p}k\otimes\partial^{L}_{q}(\ell),\qquad k\in K_{p},\ \ell\in L_{q},\ p+q=n. $$

Since we will always be working over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ , we may neglect the $(-1)^{p}$ factor.

### F Lifted product codes: homological algebra viewpoint

We now explain how the lifted product code construction arises from tensor products of $\mathcal{R}$ -module chain complexes. Let $A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ and $B\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}$ be the classical base matrices associated with our lifted product code. We associate to $A$ the two-term complex of right $\mathcal{R}$ -modules

$$ C_{\bullet}^{A}:\qquad C^{A}_{1}=\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{A}=A\;}C^{A}_{0}=\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}}. $$

We view the elements of $C^{A}_{1}$ and $C^{A}_{0}$ as column vectors and the boundary map is defined by left multiplication by $A$ . This is compatible with the right $\mathcal{R}$ -module structure and defines a valid homomorphism between right $\mathcal{R}$ -modules: for every $x\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}$ and $r\in\mathcal{R}$ ,

$$ \partial_{A}(xr)=A(xr)=(Ax)r=\partial_{A}(x)r. $$

We may similarly associate a two-term complex to $B$ . However, since the tensor product of chain complexes is only well-defined between a right-module complex and a left-module complex, we will instead consider the left-module complex given by the dual of $C_{\bullet}^{B}$ :

$$ \hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}:\qquad\hat{C}_{1}^{B}={}_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}\xrightarrow{\;\hat{\partial}_{B}=B^{*}\;}\hat{C}_{0}^{B}={}_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}} $$

Here the matrix $B^{*}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}\times r_{2}}$ defines a homomorphism of free left $\mathcal{R}$ -modules via the coordinate formula

$$ (B^{*}y)_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r_{2}}y_{j}(B^{*})_{ij},\qquad y\in{}_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}. $$

This produces a valid homomorphism since for every $y\in{}_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}$ and $r\in\mathcal{R}$ , we have

$$ (B^{*}(ry))_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r_{2}}(ry_{j})(B^{*})_{ij}=r\sum_{j=1}^{r_{2}}y_{j}(B^{*})_{ij}=r(B^{*}y)_{i}. $$

We can now form the tensor product complex

$$ Q_{\bullet}\coloneqq C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B} $$

associated to the lifted product code $\textrm{LP}(A,B)$ . Since both $C_{\bullet}^{A}$ and $\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}$ are two-term complexes, $Q_{\bullet}$ is the three-term complex given as follows:

$$ Q_{2}\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{2}\;}Q_{1}\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{1}\;}Q_{0}. $$

Its three nonzero chain groups are

$$ \displaystyle Q_{2} \displaystyle=C_{1}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{1}^{B}=\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}\cong\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}r_{2}}, \displaystyle Q_{1} \displaystyle=\left(C_{1}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{0}^{B}\right)\oplus\left(C_{0}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{1}^{B}\right) \displaystyle=\left(\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}}\right)\oplus\left(\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}\right)\cong\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}c_{2}}\oplus\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}r_{2}}, \displaystyle Q_{0} \displaystyle=C_{0}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{0}^{B}=\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}}\cong\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}c_{2}}. $$

After expanding each copy of $\mathcal{R}$ as a binary vector space of dimension $|G|$ , the middle term $Q_{1}$ has

$$ |G|\,(c_{1}c_{2}+r_{1}r_{2}) $$

binary coordinates. These correspond to the physical qubits of the lifted product code.

We now compute the two boundary maps of $Q_{\bullet}$ which correspond to the $X$ and $Z$ parity check matrices. First consider

$$ \partial_{1}:Q_{1}\longrightarrow Q_{0}. $$

Using the definition of the tensor product boundary map in (47), for $x\in C_{1}^{A}$ , $z\in\hat{C}_{0}^{B}$ , $u\in C_{0}^{A}$ , and $y\in\hat{C}_{1}^{B}$ , we have

$$ \partial_{1}\bigl((x\otimes z)\oplus(u\otimes y)\bigr)=Ax\otimes z+u\otimes B^{*}y. $$

The first term applies $A$ to the $C^{A}_{1}$ factor and leaves the $\hat{C}_{0}^{B}$ factor unchanged. This corresponds to the block matrix

$$ A\otimes I_{c_{2}}. $$

Since $A$ acts by left multiplication on the group-ring entries, its binary expansion is

$$ L(A\otimes I_{c_{2}}). $$

The second term leaves the $C_{0}^{A}$ factor unchanged and applies the left-module map corresponding to $B^{*}$ to the $\hat{C}_{1}^{B}$ factor. By the coordinate convention for left modules in (51), for $y\in C_{1}^{B}\cong\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}$

$$ (B^{*}y)_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r_{2}}y_{j}(B^{*})_{ij}. $$

This corresponds to usual matrix multiplication except with the entries of $B^{*}$ acting on the right. After binary expansion, this map is represented by $R(B^{*})$ . Including the unchanged $C_{0}^{A}$ factor, the second block of $\partial_{1}$ is therefore

$$ R(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{*}). $$

Hence the binary matrix representing $\partial_{1}$ is

$$ H_{X}=\bigl[L(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})\;\big|\;R(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{*})\bigr], $$

which agrees with the $X$ -check matrix in Definition 10.

Next consider

$$ \partial_{2}:Q_{2}\longrightarrow Q_{1}. $$

With the ordering of $Q_{1}$ used in (56), namely

$$ Q_{1}=\left(C_{1}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{0}^{B}\right)\oplus\left(C_{0}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{1}^{B}\right), $$

the definition for the tensor product boundary map in (47) gives

$$ \partial_{2}(x\otimes y)=\left(x\otimes B^{*}y,\;Ax\otimes y\right) $$

for $x\in C_{1}^{A}$ and $y\in\hat{C}_{1}^{B}$ . The first component applies the left-module map $y\mapsto B^{*}y$ to the second factor, so its binary expansion is

$$ R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B^{*}). $$

The second component applies $A$ to the first factor, so its binary expansion is

$$ L(A\otimes I_{r_{2}}). $$

Hence, as a binary matrix, $\partial_{2}$ has the block form

$$ \partial_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B^{*})\\
L(A\otimes I_{r_{2}})\end{bmatrix} $$

and so

$$ H_{Z}=\partial_{2}^{T}=\bigl[R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B^{*})^{\,T}\;\big|\;L(A\otimes I_{r_{2}})^{\,T}\bigr]=\bigl[R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B)\;\big|\;L(A^{*}\otimes I_{r_{2}})\bigr] $$

which agrees with the $Z$ -check matrix in Definition 10. Therefore, the lifted product code associated with $(A,B)$ is exactly the CSS code corresponding to the tensor product complex

$$ Q_{\bullet}=C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}:\qquad Q_{2}\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{2}\;}Q_{1}\xrightarrow{\;\partial_{1}\;}Q_{0}. $$

The physical qubits correspond to $Q_{1}$ and the $X$ and $Z$ stabilizers correspond to $Q_{0}$ and $Q_{2}$ respectively.

## Appendix B Canonical basis for lifted product codes

In this appendix, we explain the general procedure to construct explicit low-weight representatives for the single-qubit $X$ and $Z$ logical operators of our codes. By this we mean that the representatives satisfy the canonical commutation relation $[X_{i},Z_{j}]=2X_{i}Z_{j}\delta_{ij}$ or equivalently $X_{i}\cdot Z_{j}=\delta_{ij}$ where the dot product denotes the binary symplectic inner product. We refer to this collection of representatives as a canonical basis for the logical operators.

### A Setup

We begin by characterizing sufficient conditions for a collection of $X$ -type and $Z$ -type operators to form a canonical basis and then define the square-invertibility condition which is needed for our construction of a canonical basis for lifted product codes.

#### 1 Canonical logical bases

We begin by establishing a simple lemma that provides a set of sufficient conditions for identifying a collection of $X$ -type and $Z$ -type operators as a canonical basis for a CSS code.

#### Lemma 1.

Let $H_{X},H_{Z}$ be the parity-check matrices of a CSS code with $k$ logical qubits. Identify $X$ -type and $Z$ -type Pauli operators with their binary support vectors in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ . Suppose we have a collection $\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ and $\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ of such operators satisfying

$$ X_{i}\in\ker H_{Z},\qquad Z_{i}\in\ker H_{X}\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,k, $$

and

$$ X_{i}\cdot Z_{j}=\delta_{ij} $$

where the dot denotes the $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ inner product. Then $X_{i}$ and $Z_{i}$ are single-qubit $X$ and $Z$ logical operators for the $i$ -th logical qubit.

#### Proof.

For a CSS code, an $X$ -type operator commutes with all $Z$ -stabilizers precisely when its binary support lies in $\ker H_{Z}$ . To show that $X_{i}$ is a nontrivial logical operator, it remains to show that it is not an $X$ -stabilizer, i.e. that $X_{i}\notin\operatorname{row}(H_{X})$ .

Suppose, for contradiction, that $X_{i}\in\operatorname{row}(H_{X})$ . Let $h_{1},\ldots,h_{m}$ be the rows of $H_{X}$ . Then there exist coefficients $c_{1},\ldots,c_{m}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ such that

$$ X_{i}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}c_{a}h_{a}. $$

Since $Z_{j}\in\ker H_{X}$ , we have

$$ h_{a}\cdot Z_{j}=0\qquad\text{for every }a=1,\ldots,m. $$

Hence we have

$$ X_{i}\cdot Z_{j}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}c_{a}(h_{a}\cdot Z_{j})=0 $$

for all $Z_{j}$ . This contradicts the assumption that $X_{i}\cdot Z_{j}=\delta_{ij}$ , so we conclude that $X_{i}\notin\operatorname{row}(H_{X})$ , and hence $X_{i}$ is a nontrivial logical operator. A similar argument shows that all the $Z_{i}$ are nontrivial logical operators as well. Since they satisfy the canonical commutation relation (60), they are the single-qubit $X$ and $Z$ logical operators for the $k$ logical qubits. ∎

We take the most general definition of a canonical logical basis to be a collection of $X$ -type and $Z$ -type representatives satisfying the conditions of Lemma 1. The canonical basis we will construct for non-abelian lifted product codes enjoys three additional properties beyond this pairing: its representatives are built directly from classical codewords of the base matrices, the logical operators within a basis are related by group action, and the supports of conjugate pairs intersect on exactly one data qubit.

#### 2 Square-invertibility condition

Let $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , and let

$$ A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}},\qquad B\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}, $$

with $r_{1}<c_{1}$ and $r_{2}<c_{2}$ , be the classical base matrices defining the lifted product code $\textrm{LP}(A,B)$ . The following definition captures the assumptions we will make about the structure of $A$ and $B$ .

#### Definition 16 (Square invertibility condition).

Let $M\in\mathcal{R}^{r\times c}$ with $r<c$ . We say that $M$ satisfies the square invertibility condition with respect to a chosen binary expansion of $\mathcal{R}$ if, after possibly reordering its columns, $M$ can be written as

$$ M=\bigl[M_{\mathrm{free}}\mid M_{\mathrm{pivot}}\bigr], $$

where

$$ M_{\mathrm{free}}\in\mathcal{R}^{r\times(c-r)},\qquad M_{\mathrm{pivot}}\in\mathcal{R}^{r\times r}, $$

and the binary expansion of $M_{\mathrm{pivot}}$ is an invertible matrix over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ . We call the first $c-r$ columns the free columns and the last $r$ columns the pivot columns.

After possibly reordering columns, we can fix decompositions

$$ A=\bigl[A_{\mathrm{free}}\mid A_{\mathrm{pivot}}\bigr],\qquad B=\bigl[B_{\mathrm{free}}\mid B_{\mathrm{pivot}}\bigr], $$

where

$$ A_{\mathrm{pivot}}\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times r_{1}},\qquad B_{\mathrm{pivot}}\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times r_{2}}, $$

and $L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}})$ and $R(B_{\mathrm{pivot}})$ are invertible binary matrices. Letting

$$ f_{A}\coloneqq c_{1}-r_{1},\qquad f_{B}\coloneqq c_{2}-r_{2}, $$

the decompositions in (61) induce coordinate splittings

$$ \mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}=\mathcal{R}^{f_{A}}\oplus\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}},\qquad\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}}=\mathcal{R}^{f_{B}}\oplus\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}. $$

We refer to the first summand as the free coordinates and to the second summand as the pivot coordinates. Throughout this section, we will assume that $A$ satisfies the square invertibility condition (Definition 16) with respect to the left regular representation, and that $B$ satisfies the square invertibility condition with respect to the right regular representation.

### B Main result

We now state the main result of this section: an explicit canonical logical basis for the lifted product code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ . The construction of this basis exploits the product structure of the code; each logical representative is derived from a codeword of one of the classical base codes. Logical $X$ operators arise from codewords of $B$ and logical $Z$ operators arise from codewords of $A$ . The key step is choosing suitable bases for the two classical codes.

The square invertibility condition (Definition 16) ensures that $A$ and $B$ admit bases in which each basis codeword is supported on exactly one of the free coordinates, a distinct one for each codeword. After padding with zeros, these classical basis vectors become logical $X$ and $Z$ representatives that pair up canonically – within each pair, the supports of $X$ and $Z$ overlap on exactly one physical qubit (hence the operators anticommute), while operators from different pairs have disjoint support (and therefore commute).

The basis is built from distinguished codewords of the two classical factor codes, which we now define. For $1\leq\alpha\leq f_{A}$ and $g\in G$ , let $\epsilon_{A}^{\alpha}(g)\in\mathcal{R}^{f_{A}}$ denote the vector with $g$ in the $\alpha$ -th coordinate and zero elsewhere. Similarly, for $1\leq\beta\leq f_{B}$ , let $\epsilon_{B}^{\beta}(g)\in\mathcal{R}^{f_{B}}$ denote the vector with $g$ in the $\beta$ -th coordinate and zero elsewhere. We first define the kernel vectors. Let

$$ v_{A}^{\alpha,g}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}\quad\left(\text{resp. }v_{B}^{\beta,g}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}}\right) $$

be the unique element of $\ker L(A)$ (resp. $\ker R(B)$ ) whose free part is $\epsilon_{A}^{\alpha}(g)$ (resp. $\epsilon_{B}^{\beta}(g)$ ); its pivot part is uniquely determined because $L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}})$ (resp. $R(B_{\mathrm{pivot}})$ ) is invertible (Lemma 2). Likewise, let

$$ w_{A}^{\alpha,g}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}\quad\left(\text{resp. }w_{B}^{\beta,g}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}}\right) $$

be the vector whose free part is $\epsilon_{A}^{\alpha}(g)$ (resp. $\epsilon_{B}^{\beta}(g)$ ) and whose pivot part is zero; it is the unique representative of its class in $\operatorname{coker}L(A^{*})$ (resp. $\operatorname{coker}R(B^{*})$ ) supported only on the free coordinates (Lemma 2). The canonical logical basis for $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ is characterized by the following theorem.

#### Theorem 4 (Canonical basis of logical operators).

Let $A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ and $B\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}$ satisfy the square invertibility condition (Definition 16) with respect to the left and right regular representations, respectively. For $1\leq\alpha\leq f_{A}$ , $1\leq\beta\leq f_{B}$ , and $g\in G$ , define

$$ Z_{\alpha,\beta}^{g}\coloneqq\left(\mathtt{b}(v_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}w_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}}),\,0\right), $$

and

$$ X_{\alpha,\beta}^{g}\coloneqq\left(\mathtt{b}(w_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}v_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}}),\,0\right). $$

These operators form a canonical logical basis for the $k=f_{A}f_{B}|G|$ logical qubits of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ .

#### Remark 3.

For our mitten codes we have $f_{A}=f_{B}=1$ , so we may drop the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ subscripts and simply label the $X$ and $Z$ logical operators by the group elements of $G$ . The logical operators of one basis are all related to each other via group action. For example, for $X$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle X^{g} \displaystyle=\left(\mathtt{b}(w_{A}^{g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}v_{B}^{e}),0\right) \displaystyle=\left(\mathtt{b}(g\,w_{A}^{e}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}v_{B}^{e}),0\right) \displaystyle=g\cdot X^{e}. $$

where the action $g\cdot$ is defined via the last equality. A similar relationship holds for the $Z$ logicals, with the group element acting by right multiplication instead: $Z^{g}=Z^{e}\cdot g$ .

The rest of this section is devoted to proving Theorem 4. We first introduce the four binary vector spaces from which the logical operators will be constructed. For the remainder of this section, we will identify $\mathcal{R}^{m}$ with its binary expansion $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|m}$ . Define the kernels

$$ V_{A}\coloneqq\ker L(A)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|c_{1}},\qquad V_{B}\coloneqq\ker R(B)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|c_{2}} $$

and the cokernels

$$ W_{A}\coloneqq\operatorname{coker}L(A^{*})=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|c_{1}}/\im L(A^{*}),\qquad W_{B}\coloneqq\operatorname{coker}R(B^{*})=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|c_{2}}/\im R(B^{*}). $$

Under the square invertibility condition, the elements of these four spaces can be expressed in a particularly simple form.

#### Lemma 2.

Assume $A$ and $B$ satisfy the square invertibility condition. Then:

- 1. every element of $V_{A}$ and $V_{B}$ is uniquely determined by its free coordinates;

- 2. every equivalence class in $W_{A}$ and $W_{B}$ has a unique representative supported only on the free coordinates.

#### Proof.

We prove the two statements for $A$ . The proof for $B$ is identical, with left representations replaced by right representations.

First, consider the kernel. Using the decomposition

$$ \mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|c_{1}}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|f_{A}}\oplus\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|r_{1}} $$

into free and pivot coordinates, write

$$ v=\begin{pmatrix}x\\
y\end{pmatrix},\qquad x\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|f_{A}},\qquad y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|r_{1}}. $$

Then $v\in V_{A}=\ker L(A)$ means

$$ L(A_{\mathrm{free}})x+L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}})y=0. $$

Since $L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}})$ is invertible over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ , the pivot part $y$ is uniquely determined by the free part $x$ . Hence, every element of $V_{A}$ is uniquely determined by its free coordinates.

Next, consider the cokernel

$$ W_{A}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|c_{1}}/\im L(A^{*}). $$

Let

$$ w=\begin{pmatrix}x\\
y\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|c_{1}},\qquad x\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|f_{A}},\qquad y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|r_{1}}. $$

We want to replace $w$ by an equivalent representative whose pivot part is zero. Since representatives in the same equivalence class may differ by an element of $\im L(A^{*})$ , we may add a vector of the form

$$ L(A^{*})u,\qquad u\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|r_{1}}. $$

Hence,

$$ w+L(A^{*})u=\begin{pmatrix}x+L(A_{\mathrm{free}}^{*})u\\
y+L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}}^{*})u\end{pmatrix}. $$

Because $L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}})$ is invertible, so is $L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}}^{*})$ , and so there is a unique $u\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|r_{1}}$ such that

$$ y+L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}}^{*})u=0. $$

For this choice of $u$ , the representative $w+L(A^{*})u$ is supported only on the free coordinates. Hence, every equivalence class in $W_{A}$ has a free-supported representative.

It remains to show this representative is unique. Suppose two free-supported vectors belong to the same equivalence class in $W_{A}$ . Their difference is again free-supported and lies in $\im L(A^{*})$ , so is equal to $L(A^{*})u$ for some $u\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|r_{1}}$ . Looking at the pivot coordinates gives

$$ L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}}^{*})u=0 $$

which implies $u=0$ since $L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}}^{*})$ is invertible. This proves uniqueness. ∎

By Lemma 2, the vectors $v_{A}^{\alpha,g}$ , $w_{A}^{\alpha,g}$ , $v_{B}^{\beta,g}$ , and $w_{B}^{\beta,g}$ defined before Theorem 4 are well defined. Moreover, the binary expansions $\mathtt{b}(v_{A}^{\alpha,g})$ and $\mathtt{b}(v_{B}^{\beta,g})$ form bases of $V_{A}$ and $V_{B}$ , and the equivalence classes of $\mathtt{b}(w_{A}^{\alpha,g})$ and $\mathtt{b}(w_{B}^{\beta,g})$ form bases of $W_{A}$ and $W_{B}$ , respectively. The logical operators of Theorem 4 are tensor products of these vectors, lifted to their binary representation. Since we are taking tensor products over $\mathcal{R}$ , we recall that they satisfy the balancing relation

$$ ug\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}v=u\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}gv\quad\text{for all }u\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}},v\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}},g\in G $$

by construction. Hence, a tensor product of the form $v_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}w_{B}^{\beta,h}$ is uniquely specified by the group element $gh$ and so we will work with the convention that the group label is always placed on the $A$ -side and the identity element $e_{G}$ is placed on the $B$ -side. We also adopt the convention that $A\otimes I_{c_{2}}$ acts on the first tensor factor by the left action, $(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})(u\otimes v)=(Au)\otimes v$ , while $I_{c_{1}}\otimes B$ acts on the second factor by the right action, $(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=u\otimes(vB)$ .

We can now prove Theorem 4.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.

Our strategy will be to show that the $X$ -type and $Z$ -type representatives defined above satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 1. By Definition 10, the physical qubits of $\mathrm{LP}(A,B)$ are indexed by the binary expansion of

$$ \left(\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{c_{2}}\right)\oplus\left(\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}}\right). $$

The representatives defined in Eqs. (62) and (63) have support only on the first block. We first show that the $Z$ -type representatives commute with all $X$ -stabilizers and the $X$ -type representatives commute with all $Z$ -stabilizers. Using the block form of $H_{X}$ from (23), we get

$$ H_{X}\left(\mathtt{b}(v_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}w_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}}),\,0_{r_{1}r_{2}|G|}\right)=L(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})\,\mathtt{b}(v_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}w_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}})=\mathtt{b}(Av_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}w_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}})=0, $$

because $\mathtt{b}(v_{A}^{\alpha,g})\in V_{A}=\ker L(A)$ . Hence, $Z_{\alpha,\beta}^{g}\in\ker H_{X}.$ Similarly, using the block form of $H_{Z}$ from (24), we get

$$ H_{Z}\left(\mathtt{b}(w_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}v_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}}),\,0_{r_{1}r_{2}|G|}\right)=R(I_{c_{1}}\otimes B)\,\mathtt{b}(w_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}v_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}})=\mathtt{b}(w_{A}^{\alpha,g}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}(v_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}}B))=0, $$

because $\mathtt{b}(v_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}})\in V_{B}=\ker R(B)$ . Hence, $X_{\alpha,\beta}^{g}\in\ker H_{Z}.$

It remains to compute the symplectic pairing. The free part of $v_{A}^{\alpha,g}$ is $\epsilon_{A}^{\alpha}(g)$ , while $w_{A}^{\alpha^{\prime},g^{\prime}}$ is supported only on the free coordinates with free part $\epsilon_{A}^{\alpha^{\prime}}(g^{\prime})$ . Therefore,

$$ \mathtt{b}(v_{A}^{\alpha,g})\cdot\mathtt{b}(w_{A}^{\alpha^{\prime},g^{\prime}})=\delta_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}\delta_{g,g^{\prime}}. $$

Similarly, the free part of $v_{B}^{\beta^{\prime},e_{G}}$ is $\epsilon_{B}^{\beta^{\prime}}(e_{G})$ , while $w_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}}$ is supported only on the free coordinates with free part $\epsilon_{B}^{\beta}(e_{G})$ . Hence,

$$ \mathtt{b}(w_{B}^{\beta,e_{G}})\cdot\mathtt{b}(v_{B}^{\beta^{\prime},e_{G}})=\delta_{\beta,\beta^{\prime}}. $$

Consequently,

$$ X_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime}}^{g^{\prime}}\cdot Z_{\alpha,\beta}^{g}=\delta_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}\delta_{\beta,\beta^{\prime}}\delta_{g,g^{\prime}}. $$

Hence, the hypotheses of Lemma 1 are satisfied and so the operators

$$ \left\{X_{\alpha,\beta}^{g},Z_{\alpha,\beta}^{g}\right\}_{1\leq\alpha\leq f_{A},\;1\leq\beta\leq f_{B},\;g\in G} $$

form a canonical basis for the $k=f_{A}f_{B}|G|$ single-qubit $X$ and $Z$ logical operators of $\mathrm{LP}(A,B)$ . ∎

### C Aside on connection to Künneth formula

One might notice that our canonical logical basis and its product structure is suspiciously reminiscent of the Künneth formula. This is not a coincidence, but rather a direct consequence of the square invertibility condition. We now explain this connection.

For a general group algebra $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , the homology of the tensor product complex $C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}$ usually does not reduce to a direct sum of the tensor products of the homology of the two factors like in the standard Künneth formula. It is instead computed by the Künneth spectral sequence [108]:

$$ \displaystyle E^{2}_{p,q}=\bigoplus_{i+j=q}\Tor_{p}^{\mathcal{R}}\!\left(H_{i}(C_{\bullet}^{A}),\,H_{j}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})\right)\;\Longrightarrow\;H_{p+q}\!\left(C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}\right). $$

The symbol $\Longrightarrow$ indicates that $E^{2}$ is only the starting page; successive pages are obtained by taking homology with respect to differentials:

$$ d^{r}:E^{r}_{p,q}\longrightarrow E^{r}_{p-r,q+r-1},\qquad E^{r+1}_{p,q}=\frac{\ker\!\left(d^{r}:E^{r}_{p,q}\to E^{r}_{p-r,q+r-1}\right)}{\operatorname{im}\!\left(d^{r}:E^{r}_{p+r,q-r+1}\to E^{r}_{p,q}\right)}. $$

The limiting page $E^{\infty}$ then assembles along the diagonals $p+q=n$ into $H_{n}(C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})$ . Since $\Tor_{0}^{\mathcal{R}}(M,N)=M\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}N$ , the $p=0$ column contains the ordinary tensor-product terms of the form $H_{i}(C_{\bullet}^{A})\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}H_{j}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})$ . We will show that the square invertibility condition makes the spectral sequence collapse immediately at the $E^{2}$ page so that these ordinary tensor-product terms are the only ones that contribute to the homology of the product complex.

First, we identify the homologies of the two factors. Recall that for the complex

$$ C_{\bullet}^{A}:\quad\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}\xrightarrow{\;A\;}\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}} $$

the square invertibility condition tells us that $A$ can be decomposed as $A=[\,A_{\mathrm{free}}\mid A_{\mathrm{pivot}}\,]$ where $L(A_{\mathrm{pivot}})$ is invertible over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ . Hence, the equation

$$ A_{\mathrm{free}}x+A_{\mathrm{pivot}}y=0 $$

can be solved uniquely for $y$ given any choice of $x$ , yielding

$$ H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})=\ker A\cong\mathcal{R}^{f_{A}},\qquad H_{0}(C_{\bullet}^{A})=\operatorname{coker}A=0. $$

Similarly, since the square invertibility condition also holds for $B$ , for the dual complex $\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}$ defined in (50) we have

$$ H_{1}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})=0,\qquad H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})\cong\mathcal{R}^{f_{B}}. $$

Note that the two nonzero homology modules $H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})$ and $H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})$ are free.

Plugging these into the spectral sequence, only one entry survives. Every summand involving $H_{0}(C_{\bullet}^{A})$ or $H_{1}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})$ vanishes, and freeness of $H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})$ and $H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})$ forces all higher Tor to vanish as well:

$$ \Tor_{p}^{\mathcal{R}}\!\left(\mathcal{R}^{f_{A}},\,\mathcal{R}^{f_{B}}\right)=0\qquad\text{for all }p\geq 1. $$

Hence, the unique nonzero entry on the $E^{2}$ page is

$$ E^{2}_{0,1}\;=\;H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})\;\cong\;\mathcal{R}^{f_{A}f_{B}}, $$

so schematically the $E^{2}$ page looks like

$$ \begin{array}[]{r|cccc}q=2&0&0&0&\cdots\\
q=1&H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})&0&0&\cdots\\
q=0&0&0&0&\cdots\\
\hline\cr&p=0&p=1&p=2&\cdots\end{array}\hskip 20.00003pt. $$

The differentials touching $E^{r}_{0,1}$ have the form

$$ E^{r}_{r,\,2-r}\;\xrightarrow{\;d^{r}\;}\;E^{r}_{0,1}\;\xrightarrow{\;d^{r}\;}\;E^{r}_{-r,\,r}. $$

The entry on the right sits in column $p=-r<0$ and is zero by convention. The entry on the left is also zero on the $E^{2}$ -page: at $r=2$ it occupies the lattice point $(2,0)$ , empty in the diagram above; for $r\geq 3$ it has $q=2-r<0$ . With both neighbors zero, the outgoing $d^{r}$ has kernel all of $E^{r}_{0,1}$ and the incoming $d^{r}$ has image zero, so the recursion

$$ E^{r+1}_{0,1}\;=\;\frac{\ker\!\left(d^{r}\colon E^{r}_{0,1}\to 0\right)}{\im\!\left(d^{r}\colon 0\to E^{r}_{0,1}\right)}\;=\;\frac{E^{r}_{0,1}}{0}\;=\;E^{r}_{0,1} $$

holds for every $r\geq 2$ . The entry persists unchanged to $E^{\infty}$ , and we conclude

$$ H_{1}\!\left(C_{\bullet}^{A}\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}\right)=H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})\otimes_{\mathcal{R}}H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B}). $$

Hence, we may construct the $Z$ logical operators of our code by constructing a basis for $H_{1}(C_{\bullet}^{A})$ and $H_{0}(\hat{C}_{\bullet}^{B})$ . This is exactly what we did in the construction of our canonical basis. The construction of the $X$ logical operators follows similarly by looking at the first cohomology group of the tensor product complex.

## Appendix C Universal fault-tolerant quantum instruction sets

In this appendix, we provide a formal definition of the notion of a universal fault-tolerant quantum instruction set. We then more formally define the three instruction sets we considered in the main text and explain how they enable universal quantum computation.

Consider a qLDPC processor based on a CSS code with parameters $\llbracket n,k,d\rrbracket$ together with a fixed decoder. An instruction is a logical operation on the processor’s logical qubits together with a physical gadget that realizes the operation.

#### Definition 17 (Universal fault-tolerant quantum instruction set (formal version of Definition 1)).

Consider a qLDPC processor with $k$ logical qubits. A set of fault-tolerant instructions $\mathcal{I}$ is a universal fault-tolerant quantum instruction set for the processor if every unitary $U$ on the $k$ logical qubits can be realized to any precision $\epsilon>0$ by a finite sequence of instructions from $\mathcal{I}$ [109], where

- 1. each instruction may be chosen adaptively, conditioned on the classical record of earlier measurement outcomes, and

- 2. the combined action of the sequence is required to equal $U$ only up to a Pauli frame determined by that record.

An example of a universal instruction set is the collection of two-qubit CNOTs together with the single-qubit Hadamard and $T$ gates [63]. Universality, however, does not require unitary gadgets; measurements and state injection suffice, as the constructions below show.

#### Definition 18 (Basic instruction set $\mathcal{I}_{B}$ ).

The basic instruction set consists of (i) the single-qubit logical Pauli measurements $\{\bar{X}_{i},\bar{Y}_{i},\bar{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ , (ii) the weight-two logical Pauli-product measurements $\{\bar{X}_{i}\bar{X}_{j},\bar{Z}_{i}\bar{Z}_{j}\}_{1\leq i<j\leq k}$ , and (iii) noisy $T$ -state injection i.e. the preparation of a designated logical qubit in the state $T\ket{+}$ up to a known Pauli correction, with an injection error rate set by the physical noise.

The Clifford group together with the $T$ gate forms a universal gate set [63, 64]. Moreover, any Clifford+ $T$ circuit can be compiled into a Pauli-based computation consisting of stabilizer-state preparations, adaptive logical Pauli-product measurements, and the consumption of logical $\ket{T}$ states [65]. Noisy logical $\ket{T}$ states are injected using instruction (iii) and are then distilled. Provided the input error lies below the distillation threshold and the logical stabilizer operations are sufficiently reliable, magic-state distillation can reduce the output error below any target $\epsilon>0$ with overhead polylogarithmic in $1/\epsilon$ [64, 67, 110]. The distillation circuit may be implemented either using transversal CNOT gates between separate encoded blocks or, when a single block encodes many logical qubits, as a sequence of logical Pauli-product measurements within that block [68]. A distilled $\ket{T}$ state is then consumed via gate teleportation to implement the logical $T$ gate [64, 22]. These ingredients are standard; what is specific to the mitten codes is that every instruction in $\mathcal{I}_{B}$ is implemented using only five reusable gadgets (Section IV, Table 2).

#### Definition 19 (High-throughput instruction set $\mathcal{I}_{H}$ ).

The high-throughput instruction set consists of (i) parallel logical Pauli-product measurement i.e. the joint fault-tolerant measurement of a set of commuting logical Pauli products in a single gadget, and (ii) parallel $T$ -state injection i.e. the simultaneous injection of noisy $T$ states into all $k$ logical qubits of a block.

#### Definition 20 (Fixed-gadget instruction set $\mathcal{I}_{F}$ ).

The fixed-gadget instruction set consists of (i) the extractor measurement, i.e., the fault-tolerant measurement of an arbitrary logical Pauli product, and (ii) noisy $T$ -state injection. The extractor is a single fixed gadget: its qubit layout and connectivity are fixed in hardware, and the Pauli product to be measured is selected in software by switching the appropriate connections on or off.

Every instruction of the basic instruction set $\mathcal{I}_{B}$ can be viewed as a special case of an instruction of the other two sets. Therefore, both $\mathcal{I}_{H}$ and $\mathcal{I}_{F}$ are universal fault-tolerant quantum instruction sets.

## Appendix D Surgery

*Figure 5: Surgery gadgets. (a) The seed graph surgery gadgets for measuring logical $\bar{X}$ / $\bar{Z}$ operators constructed based on the group-structured canonical logical basis (Appendix B) where different logical operators are related by group action $g$ and the seed gadgets can be used to measure all $|G|$ of them within an orbit by rewiring. (b) $\bar{X}\bar{X}$ , $\bar{Z}\bar{Z}$ and $\bar{Y}$ graph surgery gadgets constructed by bridging the seed gadgets from (a). Together, the graph surgery gadgets in (a) and (b) can generate the entire Clifford group. (c) Parallel surgery gadget for measuring Pauli products in parallel. (d) Full extractor for measuring arbitrary weight Pauli product operators using a fixed gadget.*

Universal quantum computation can be achieved with Clifford gates and non-Clifford magic state inputs [64, 65]. On qLDPC codes, Clifford computation can be implemented through logical Pauli-product measurements (PPMs) generated via code surgery [73, 52, 75, 77, 76]. Code surgery realizes PPMs on general qLDPC codes by attaching ancillary qubits and checks that couple to the targeted logical operators. This temporarily enlarges the original code into a merged code in which the targeted logical operators become stabilizers. Their measurement outcomes are inferred from syndrome extraction on the merged code.

More concretely, the merged code is a stabilizer code on the original data qubits and the ancilla qubits of the surgery gadget. Its checks comprise the original checks, some extended onto the ancilla qubits, and additional checks introduced by the gadget. We design these extensions and additional checks so that the merged code preserves the distance of the original code while keeping both the number of qubits in each check and the number of checks acting on each qubit as small as possible. For the $X$ -type graph surgery described below, the protocol proceeds in three steps, which we first describe in the absence of faults. First, the gadget ancilla qubits are initialized in $\ket{0}$ , preserving the eigenvalues of the original $Z$ -checks when they are extended onto the ancillas. Second, the merged-code checks are measured for a number of syndrome extraction rounds proportional to the original code distance $d$ . Although the individual new $X$ -check outcomes can be random, a specified product of these checks equals the targeted logical operator, so the corresponding product of outcomes gives the logical measurement result. Third, the ancilla qubits are measured in the $Z$ basis and syndrome extraction resumes on the original code. Each restored $Z$ -check eigenvalue is the product of its deformed-check eigenvalue and the final $Z$ -measurement outcomes on the ancillas to which it was extended. With noise, the full measurement record, including the preparation and readout boundaries, is decoded to infer the logical measurement result and the corrections to track in the Pauli frame. The $Z$ -type protocol exchanges $X$ and $Z$ , using $\ket{+}$ preparation and $X$ -basis readout [75, 77]. Preparation and readout for mixed-type gadgets depend on their construction.

The remainder of this appendix is organized as follows. In Appendix D.A we construct the graph surgery gadgets $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ , $\mathbf{S}_{Y}$ , $\mathbf{S}_{Z}$ , $\mathbf{S}_{XX}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{ZZ}$ , measuring logical $\bar{X}$ , $\bar{Y}$ , $\bar{Z}$ , $\bar{X}\bar{X}$ and $\bar{Z}\bar{Z}$ , respectively for mitten codes (Figure 5(a,b)). An unstructured canonical logical basis would require one dedicated gadget per measured operator, which means $2k$ seed gadgets for the basis single qubit $\bar{X}$ and $\bar{Z}$ operators and, from them, $3k+k(k-1)$ distinct gadgets to support full Clifford processing. The group structure of the canonical basis of mitten codes (Appendix B) reduces this to $5$ reusable gadgets generated from only $2$ seed gadgets, $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{Z}$ . Rewiring a seed gadget by the group action allows it to measure any other logical qubit, as illustrated in Figure 5(a). Bridging seed gadgets produces the remaining three gadgets. In Appendix D.B we construct parallel surgery gadgets (Figure 5(c)), which measure many logical Pauli products on a single merged code to support high-throughput Clifford processing. Because the canonical basis arises from the two classical factor codes, all canonical $X$ ( $Z$ ) representatives, and hence the $X$ -side ( $Z$ -side) parallel gadgets, are supported on only $2$ of the $5$ blocks of data qubits, $D_{1}\cup D_{2}$ ( $D_{1}\cup D_{3}$ ) of mitten codes, reducing the overhead of the parallel surgery gadget. In Appendix D.C we construct and bridge an $X$ -side and a $Z$ -side extractor into a full extractor (Figure 5(d)), which is a single fixed gadget measuring arbitrary logical Pauli products [59, 71]; this supports the fixed-gadget instruction set. Finally, Appendix D.D collects the expansion conditions under which all these gadgets preserve the code distance, and the methods we use to certify them. Throughout, every construction is presented concretely for the mitten codes, whose canonical basis $\{\bar{X}_{g},\bar{Z}_{g}\}_{g\in G}$ consists of a single orbit pair (Theorem 1). We also explain at the end of each subsection how the constructions generalize to LP codes of other base-matrix shapes.

### A Graph surgery

We construct graph surgery gadgets for fault-tolerant measurements of individually selected logical $\bar{X}$ , $\bar{Y}$ , $\bar{Z}$ , $\bar{X}\bar{X}$ , and $\bar{Z}\bar{Z}$ operators. A separate gadget for each operator would require $3k+k(k-1)$ gadgets for a code with $k$ logical qubits. Their sizes also depend on the weights of the measured representatives [52, 77], which can increase when a low-weight spanning set is converted into a canonical basis.

For mitten codes, the canonical basis of Theorem 1,

$$ \{\bar{X}_{g},\bar{Z}_{g}\}_{g\in G},\qquad\bar{X}_{g}=\left(g,u_{g},0,0,0\right)^{T},\quad\bar{Z}_{g}=\left(g,0,v_{g},0,0\right)^{T}, $$

offers two advantages. The representatives are supported on only two data blocks: $D_{1}\cup D_{2}$ for $\bar{X}_{g}$ and $D_{1}\cup D_{3}$ for $\bar{Z}_{g}$ , with weights controlled by the classical factor codewords (Table 1). Each family also forms a single group orbit. We therefore construct two seed gadgets, $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{Z}$ , reuse them by rewiring, and bridge them to obtain the other three measurement types (Figure 5(a,b)).

Write $\mathbf{S}(P)$ , or $\mathbf{S}_{P}$ , for a gadget measuring a logical representative $P$ . Let $\mathbf{X}(P)$ and $\mathbf{Z}(P)$ denote the original $X$ and $Z$ checks, respectively, whose supports intersect $\supp(P)$ . We describe the $X$ -type construction; exchanging $X$ and $Z$ gives the $Z$ -type construction. For mitten codes, $\mathbf{Z}(\bar{X}_{g})$ lies in check block $Z_{0}$ , and $\mathbf{X}(\bar{Z}_{g})$ in $X_{0}$ (Equation (2)).

The construction starts with a skeleton determined by the Tanner graph between $\supp(\bar{X}_{g})$ and $\mathbf{Z}(\bar{X}_{g})$ . For each data qubit $q\in\supp(\bar{X}_{g})$ , add an $X$ -check $A_{q}$ acting on $q$ . For each original $Z$ -check $B_{z}\in\mathbf{Z}(\bar{X}_{g})$ , add an ancilla $a_{z}$ and extend $B_{z}$ to act with $Z$ on $a_{z}$ . The new check $A_{q}$ also acts with $X$ on $a_{z}$ if and only if the original check $B_{z}$ acts on $q$ . Thus, whenever $A_{q}$ and the extended check $B_{z}$ overlap on the data qubit $q$ , they also overlap on $a_{z}$ . Otherwise they are disjoint. Their overlap is therefore always even, so the new $X$ -checks commute with the extended $Z$ -checks.

Consider the product of all the new checks $A_{q}$ . On the data qubits, each $A_{q}$ contributes $X$ on its own qubit $q$ , so the product acts exactly as $\bar{X}_{g}$ . It remains to show that the ancilla factors cancel. Each original $Z$ -check $B_{z}$ overlaps $\bar{X}_{g}$ on an even number of data qubits, because the two operators commute. For each of these shared qubits $q$ , the new check $A_{q}$ contributes an $X$ on the ancilla $a_{z}$ . Thus each ancilla $a_{z}$ receives an even number of $X$ factors which cancels to the identity. This holds for every ancilla, so the product of all the new checks is precisely $\bar{X}_{g}$ .

The skeleton therefore makes the target logical operator accessible through the new check outcomes. To complete the gadget, we must also ensure that it measures no additional independent logical observables, introduces no extra encoded qubits, and preserves the code distance. We address these requirements by completing the skeleton as a connected graph, adding enough ancilla connections to protect the distance, and adding checks that constrain the ancilla system. We first explain these steps, then give the check matrices and show how the gadget can be rewired to address other logical qubits and bridged with other gadgets to measure two-body logical Pauli products.

Consider the gadget graph in which a vertex represents a new $X$ -check $A_{q}$ , and an ancilla qubit connects all the vertices whose checks act on it. Thus the skeleton ancilla $a_{z}$ is a hyperedge since it can belong to more than two new $X$ -checks. An ordinary edge represents an ancilla acted on by exactly the two $X$ -checks at its endpoints. If a skeleton ancilla already belongs to exactly two new $X$ -checks, it is already an ordinary edge and requires no replacement. If this holds for every skeleton ancilla, the skeleton is already a graph.

For an ancilla shared by more than two new $X$ -checks, a graph construction requires a replacement by edge ancillas and corresponding changes to the checks. One way to do this is as follows. Suppose, for example, $B_{z}$ meets the target support on four data qubits, whose new checks are $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3},A_{4}$ . Its skeleton ancilla is shared by all four checks. One possible replacement uses an ancilla $a_{12}$ shared by $A_{1},A_{2}$ and an ancilla $a_{34}$ shared by $A_{3},A_{4}$ , with $B_{z}$ extended onto both. Each $A_{i}$ still overlaps the extended $B_{z}$ on its data qubit and one ancilla, so the two checks commute. Each replacement ancilla now occurs in exactly two vertex checks, so its $X$ factors cancel in the product of all vertex checks. Such a pairing is possible because every skeleton hyperedge has an even number of incident vertices. Finally, we ensure that the graph is connected so that only the product of all vertex checks cancels every ancilla, giving the selected logical operator $\bar{X}_{g}$ .

Next, we also want to ensure that the merged code created by attaching the surgery gadget preserves the distance of the original code. A product of vertex checks can move part of a logical operator from the data onto the ancillas on the edges leaving the selected vertex subset. If too few such edges leave that subset, this can produce a lower-weight logical representative in the merged code. We therefore add edges to increase the graph’s expansion, which measures how many edges leave a vertex subset relative to its size, and design towards the sufficient distance-preserving condition of Appendix D.D.

After completing the graph, we constrain the degrees of freedom introduced by the ancillas to ensure that attaching the surgery gadget does not introduce extra logical qubits. A cycle is a closed loop of edges in the gadget graph. The operator $Z_{C}=\prod_{e\in C}Z_{a_{e}}$ on the ancillas of a cycle $C$ commutes with every vertex $X$ -check, because each vertex meets the cycle on zero or two edges. Unless already generated by the stabilizers, such an operator is an additional logical operator supported entirely on the gadget. We make these operators stabilizers by adding a $Z$ -check for each cycle in an independent cycle basis of the completed graph. A connected graph with $|\mathcal{V}|$ vertices and $|\mathcal{E}|$ edges has $|\mathcal{E}|-|\mathcal{V}|+1$ independent cycles. Hence, including a full cycle basis removes the extra ancilla logical degrees of freedom. The merged code then encodes $k-1$ logical qubits, with the measured $\bar{X}_{g}$ fixed as a stabilizer. During the construction we keep vertex degrees, cycle-check weights, and original-check extensions small to retain low check weights and qubit degrees.

Ordering data qubits before ancillas, the merged code has binary parity-check matrices

$$ \begin{split}H_{X}^{\mathrm{merged}}&=\bordermatrix{&[n]&\mathcal{E}\cr\text{original}&H_{X}&0\cr\mathcal{V}&\Pi&\Gamma^{T}\cr}\\
H_{Z}^{\mathrm{merged}}&=\bordermatrix{&[n]&\mathcal{E}\cr\text{original}&H_{Z}&J\cr\mathcal{C}&0&\Lambda\cr}.\end{split} $$

Here $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ are the original code’s parity-check matrices, $\mathcal{V}$ indexes the vertex $X$ -checks, $\mathcal{E}$ the edge ancillas, and $\mathcal{C}$ the chosen cycle basis. The individual block matrices are defined as follows:

- • The attachment matrix $\Pi\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathcal{V}\times n}$ records which data qubit each vertex check acts on. A skeleton row has one $1$ ; a vertex without a data attachment has a zero row.

- • The incidence matrix $\Gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{V}}$ records which vertex checks act on each ancilla. Each row has two $1$ s, one for each endpoint of the edge.

- • The extension matrix $J$ has one row per original $Z$ -check and one column per edge ancilla. Its entry $J_{s,e}$ is $1$ exactly when check $s$ is extended onto ancilla $a_{e}$ .

- • The cycle matrix $\Lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{E}}$ records the ancilla support of each new cycle $Z$ -check.

Thus the original $X$ -checks are unchanged, the original $Z$ -checks acquire their ancilla extensions, and the lower row blocks are the new vertex and cycle checks. Given $H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0$ for the original code, the remaining commutation conditions are

$$ \Lambda\Gamma=0,\qquad\Pi H_{Z}^{T}=\Gamma^{T}J^{T}. $$

The first equation expresses the constraint that every cycle check overlaps each vertex check on an even number of ancillas. The second equation says that the data overlap of each vertex check with each original $Z$ -check has the same parity as their ancilla overlap; therefore, their total overlap is even. These are the cycle and extension rules described above.

The same notation also identifies the measured observable. If $x\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathcal{V}}$ selects a set of vertex checks, their product has data support $\Pi^{T}x$ and ancilla support $\Gamma x$ . The ancilla factors cancel exactly when $\Gamma x=0$ , that is, when $x\in\ker\Gamma$ . For a connected graph, this occurs only for $x=0$ or $x=\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{V}}$ . Hence, the only nontrivial logical operator that can be measured as a product of the vertex checks is indeed only target logical operator $\bar{X}_{g}$ .

Having constructed one gadget, we now explain why it can be reused for every logical qubit. Within each data and check block, qubits and checks are labeled by group elements. A $Z$ -check labeled $s$ in $Z_{0}$ touches a data qubit labeled $q$ in $D_{i}$ , for $i\in\{1,2\}$ , exactly when $s^{-1}q$ is one of the group elements appearing in $b_{i-1}$ (Equation (2)). Thus the connection depends only on the relative group label $s^{-1}q$ . Translating the qubit label by $q\mapsto gq$ and the check label by $s\mapsto gs$ preserves this connection, since

$$ (gs)^{-1}(gq)=s^{-1}g^{-1}gq=s^{-1}q. $$

Every check therefore touches the same pattern of qubits after the relabeling.

The support of $\bar{X}_{g}$ is obtained from that of $\bar{X}_{e}$ by precisely this translation, so its attached $Z$ -checks and their connections are translated in the same way. Consequently, the seed gadget $\mathbf{S}_{X}=\mathbf{S}(\bar{X}_{e})$ can measure $\bar{X}_{g}$ by rewiring its attachments. A vertex check formerly attached to data qubit $q$ is attached to $gq$ in the same data block, and the ancilla extension of original check $s$ is transferred to check $gs$ (Figure 5(a)). All internal ancillas and checks of the gadget remain fixed. The same idea lets us reuse the seed gadget $\mathbf{S}_{Z}=\mathbf{S}(\bar{Z}_{e})$ to measure any $\bar{Z}_{g}$ , but by relabeling qubits and checks by right multiplication instead.

To measure a product $\bar{X}_{g}\bar{X}_{h}$ for distinct logical qubits, we combine two rewired $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ gadgets using the bridging construction of Refs. [52, 75]. We join their vertex sets by additional edge ancillas and add $Z$ -checks for the new independent cycles. Multiplying all vertex checks on both sides cancels the $X$ factors on every gadget ancilla and bridge ancilla, since each belongs to two vertex checks, leaving $\bar{X}_{g}\bar{X}_{h}$ and giving the joint measurement without separately measuring either factor.

The bridge must also preserve the code distance. Since the product of the vertex checks on one side is a stabilizer of the merged code, that side’s logical factor is equivalent, up to this stabilizer, to $X$ on the bridge ancillas alone. Fewer than $d$ bridge ancillas would therefore give a logical representative of weight below $d$ . At least $d$ bridge edges are necessary; the completed gadget is also subject to the distance checks of Appendix D.D. Exchanging $X$ and $Z$ gives $\mathbf{S}_{ZZ}$ . Combining $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{Z}$ for the same logical qubit uses the mixed-type bridge of Ref. [75] to measure $\bar{Y}_{g}$ . Its checks act as $X$ towards the $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ side and as $Z$ towards the $\mathbf{S}_{Z}$ side, so the merged code is not CSS. Equation (68) describes the same-type gadgets, with $X$ and $Z$ exchanged where appropriate.

The two seeds therefore generate five reusable gadget types, $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ , $\mathbf{S}_{Z}$ , $\mathbf{S}_{XX}$ , $\mathbf{S}_{ZZ}$ , and $\mathbf{S}_{Y}$ , implementing the logical Pauli measurements of the basic instruction set $\mathcal{I}_{B}$ . Each seed’s interface can be rewired independently to select the logical qubits. Table 2 reports the ancilla and check counts for the eight mitten codes, together with the maximum check weight of the merged code, which is at most $12$ compared with $9$ for the bare codes.

#### Remark 4 (Generalization of graph surgery gadgets to LP codes of general shape).

For any LP code satisfying the square invertibility condition (Definition 16), the canonical basis $\{X^{g}_{\alpha,\beta},Z^{g}_{\alpha,\beta}\}$ of Theorem 4 has $f_{A}f_{B}$ conjugate pairs of group orbits. Within each orbit, the same relabeling argument lets one seed address all representatives. The construction therefore uses one pair of $X$ and $Z$ seeds per orbit pair, rather than the single pair needed for mitten codes. The skeleton, graph completion, and bridging steps apply as above. Including the bridged gadgets gives $3f_{A}f_{B}+2f_{A}^{2}f_{B}^{2}$ reusable gadgets for the five measurement types considered here; additional row or column symmetries can reduce this number further.
