### B Parallel surgery

As illustrated in Figure 5(c), parallel surgery88 8 Also known as high-rate surgery. measures $n_{p}$ independent logical Pauli products on a single merged code. We follow the framework of Ref. [55] to support the high-throughput instruction set $\mathcal{I}_{H}$ . For mitten codes, we measure up to $k/2$ disjoint weight-two products $\bar{X}_{g}\bar{X}_{h}$ , covering all $k=|G|$ logical qubits in one parallel measurement.

As in graph surgery, each target logical operator is obtained as a product of vertex checks whose combined action on the ancilla qubits is the identity. For an ordinary edge, cancellation requires selecting both endpoint checks or neither. In a connected graph this forces the selection of all vertex checks (or none), allowing only one independent logical measurement. A hyperedge instead only needs an even number of its incident checks to be selected, so several independent products can cancel the ancillas within one connected gadget. We therefore retain the skeleton’s hyperedges.

Given the $n_{p}$ target products, we form the union of their supports and build the skeleton as in Appendix D.A. For each data qubit $q$ in this union, add an $X$ -check $A_{q}$ acting on $q$ . For each original $Z$ -check $B_{z}$ meeting the union, add an ancilla $a_{z}$ , extend $B_{z}$ onto it, and let $A_{q}$ act on $a_{z}$ whenever $B_{z}$ acts on $q$ . Each target commutes with every $B_{z}$ , so the product of the $A_{q}$ over its support cancels every ancilla and yields that target. For mitten codes, the canonical $X$ representatives lie in $D_{1}\cup D_{2}$ , so only checks in $Z_{0}$ are extended. Exchanging $X$ and $Z$ gives the $Z$ -type construction.

The merged check matrices have the block form of Equation (68). In the skeleton, $\Gamma_{z,q}=1$ exactly when $B_{z}$ acts on $q$ , and $J$ extends each $B_{z}$ onto its own ancilla. Thus $\Pi H_{Z}^{T}=\Gamma^{T}J^{T}$ holds by construction. Recall from Appendix D.A that selecting vertex checks with a vector $x$ gives a product with ancilla support $\Gamma x$ and support $\Pi^{T}x$ on the original qubits. For each target $P_{i}$ , let $x_{i}$ select the vertices attached to its support. Since $P_{i}$ commutes with every original $Z$ -check, $\Gamma x_{i}=0$ , while $\Pi^{T}x_{i}$ is the support indicator of $P_{i}$ . Thus each target corresponds to a vector in $\ker\Gamma$ , and multiplying the selected check outcomes gives its logical measurement result.

The skeleton makes the target products measurable, but it need not preserve the code distance. We therefore enlarge the gadget by adaptive thickening, following the iterative construction of Ref. [55]. Starting with the skeleton as the first layer, we search for low-weight logical operators of the merged code and add ancilla qubits with $Z$ -checks chosen to detect as many of these operators as possible. The detected operators must then acquire additional support to remain undetected. When no useful addition fits within the limits on check weights and qubit degrees, we add a new layer of $X$ -checks, each joined to its counterpart in the previous layer by an ancilla qubit. This provides room for further additions within and between layers while keeping the checks sparse. The search is repeated after each addition, so the gadget grows according to the low-weight logical operators that remain. Only the first layer attaches to the data, and the target measurements are preserved.

In our construction, we use sQetch to estimate the merged-code distance at each step and stop when the estimated distance is at most two below the original distance (Appendix D.D). The final merged codes encode $k-n_{p}$ logical qubits: the $n_{p}$ targets become stabilizers, and no extra logical qubits remain. The gadgets in Table 3 add exactly $n_{p}$ more independent checks than ancilla qubits.

For the $\llbracket 300,60,14\rrbracket$ code, we construct gadgets measuring $n_{p}\in\{10,20,30\}$ randomly chosen, independent weight-two products of canonical $X$ logical operators. Table 3 reports their overheads and estimated merged-code distances.

### C Extractor

An extractor [59] as illustrated in Figure 5(d) is a fixed ancilla system, wired to the code block once, in which individual connections can be activated or deactivated in software. Activating the connections that address a chosen logical Pauli product turns the extractor into a surgery gadget measuring exactly that product. A single fixed gadget thereby measures arbitrary logical Pauli products thereby supporting the fixed-gadget instruction set $\mathcal{I}_{F}$ . Generally, extractors are costly in space, but it was shown for hypergraph product codes that the structure of the logical basis can suppress the extractor overhead [71]. We follow the same principle where our extractors are organized around the low-weight canonical logical basis of Appendix B.

We first construct an $X$ -side and a $Z$ -side extractor, then join them into a full extractor. For mitten codes, the canonical $X$ representatives lie in $D_{1}\cup D_{2}$ , and the $Z$ -checks acting on these blocks are precisely those in $Z_{0}$ (Equation (2)). Each single-side extractor therefore attaches to only $2$ of the $5$ data blocks, which helps keep its overhead low.

We build the $X$ -side skeleton from the union of the supports of the canonical operators $\bar{X}_{g}$ , as in the previous two subsections. This union is contained in $D_{1}\cup D_{2}$ . For each qubit $q$ in the union, add a vertex $X$ -check $A_{q}$ with an available attachment to $q$ . For each original $Z$ -check $B_{z}$ meeting the union, add an ancilla $a_{z}$ and extend $B_{z}$ onto it. Let $A_{q}$ act with $X$ on $a_{z}$ exactly when $B_{z}$ acts on $q$ . Since the relevant $B_{z}$ lie in $Z_{0}$ , the skeleton has at most $2|G|$ vertex checks and at most $|G|$ ancillas.

To measure an arbitrary $X$ -type logical Pauli product $P$ , we must configure the extractor so that the appropriate connections are activated. In particular, we choose which vertex checks $A_{q}$ are attached to the data qubits of the original code and how the original checks $B_{z}$ are extended onto the ancillas. We activate the data attachment of a vertex check $A_{q}$ exactly when $q\in\supp(P)$ ; vertex checks without a data attachment keep their original ancilla factors. With this choice, multiplying all vertex checks cancels every edge ancilla contribution and leaves precisely the desired logical operator $P$ . To ensure that the resulting checks all commute, we must also modify the way the original checks $B_{z}$ act on the ancillas.

We achieve this as follows. For each ancilla $a_{z}$ , arrange the vertex $X$ -checks $A_{q}$ acting on it in a cyclic order. Remove $a_{z}$ and replace it by one new ancilla $a_{e}$ for each neighboring pair of vertex checks, including the last and first. Each new ancilla is acted on with $X$ by its two neighboring checks. Thus the checks are the vertices of a loop, and the replacement ancillas are its edges. For example, if $a_{z}$ is shared by four checks, written as $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3},A_{4}$ , the replacement uses $a_{12},a_{23},a_{34},a_{41}$ , with $a_{ij}$ shared by $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}$ . The original check $B_{z}$ has an available connection to every replacement ancilla $a_{e}$ ; the target logical Pauli product $P$ determines which of these connections are used.

With the data attachments of the vertex checks $A_{q}$ chosen to match $\supp(P)$ , we now choose the ancilla connections of each original check $B_{z}$ so that it commutes with these configured vertex checks. For each $B_{z}$ , mark the vertex $A_{q}$ for every data qubit $q$ on which both $B_{z}$ and $P$ act. At each marked vertex, $A_{q}$ and $B_{z}$ anticommute on the data qubit, so their ancilla overlap must supply a second anticommutation. The number of marked vertices is even because $B_{z}$ commutes with the full product $P$ . Pair consecutive marked vertices around the loop and extend $B_{z}$ with $Z$ on the ancillas along the paths between each pair. In the four-check example, if only $A_{1}$ and $A_{3}$ have active data attachments, the path $A_{1}$ – $A_{2}$ – $A_{3}$ gives the extension $B_{z}Z_{a_{12}}Z_{a_{23}}$ . At each path endpoint, the extended $B_{z}$ overlaps the corresponding $A_{q}$ on one data qubit and one ancilla. At each interior vertex, it overlaps $A_{q}$ on two ancillas and no data qubit. In both cases, the two checks commute because they overlap on an even number of qubits.

The loops therefore provide the paths needed to extend the original checks for any target. Before using the extractor for measurements, we complete its construction by adding edges to ensure connectedness and the expansion required to preserve the code distance. We also add cycle checks $Z_{C}$ for a full cycle basis to ensure that the ancillas introduce no additional logical qubits.

Exchanging $X$ and $Z$ gives the $Z$ -side extractor on $D_{1}\cup D_{3}$ , with original checks in $X_{0}$ .

Finally, we bridge the $X$ - and $Z$ -side extractors to obtain a single fixed extractor for arbitrary products of the canonical logical Pauli operators. Following Ref. [71], we connect the two vertices associated with each shared data qubit by a new edge ancilla.

For a chosen target $P$ , each data qubit $q\in\supp(P)$ is attached to exactly one vertex. If $q$ is shared by the two sides, we choose one of its two vertices; the other has no data attachment. The selected vertex check acts on $q$ with the corresponding factor of $P$ : $X_{q}$ , $Y_{q}$ , or $Z_{q}$ . Data qubits outside $\supp(P)$ have no active attachment.

We first specify how the checks act on the ancillas. Vertex checks act with $X$ on existing $X$ -side ancillas and with $Z$ on existing $Z$ -side ancillas. Both endpoints of each bridge act with $X$ on its ancilla. Thus a $Z$ -side vertex incident to a bridge has $Z$ on its original edges and $X$ on the bridge.

Combining these ancilla actions with the chosen data Pauli gives the full vertex check. For example, if an $X$ -side vertex acts with $X_{a}X_{b}$ on its two incident ancillas and the target contains $Z_{q}$ on its attached data qubit, its check is

$$ A_{q}=Z_{q}X_{a}X_{b}. $$

Choosing $Y_{q}$ instead gives $A_{q}=Y_{q}X_{a}X_{b}$ . Thus the joined extractor uses non-CSS checks, both at $Z$ -side bridge endpoints and when the chosen data Pauli differs from the ancilla Paulis.

The original code checks must also be extended onto ancillas so that they commute with the vertex checks. To make these extensions possible for every target, we retain each original check’s available connections to its loop ancillas. We also give each original check an available connection to the bridge ancilla at every shared data qubit in its support. These connections are fixed before choosing $P$ . They allow an extension to follow the original loop and, when necessary, cross a bridge to reach the vertex selected for a data attachment.

For each original code check $S$ , mark every vertex whose check $A_{q}$ anticommutes with $S$ on its attached data qubit. The number of marked vertices is even because $S$ commutes with the full target $P$ . Pair the corresponding vertices consecutively around the check’s original loop and join each pair along the loop. Whenever a marked vertex is on the opposite side, continue the path across its bridge. Extend the original check along these paths using $Z$ on $X$ -side and bridge ancillas and $X$ on $Z$ -side ancillas. Each path endpoint then has one data and one ancilla anticommutation, while each interior vertex has two ancilla anticommutations, so the extended check commutes with every vertex check. The fixed loops and bridges provide the required paths for every canonical logical Pauli product; only the choice of paths depends on $P$ .

To complete the construction of the full extractor, we add any further edges needed to satisfy the expansion condition of Appendix D.D, and complete the cycle checks to a full cycle basis of the joined graph. These cycle checks use $Z$ on $X$ -side and bridge ancillas and $X$ on $Z$ -side ancillas. Table 4 reports the overheads of the completed extractor.

### D Distance-preserving condition for the surgery and extractor gadgets

Throughout the construction of the surgery and extractor gadgets, we quantify fault tolerance by the distance of the merged code. Ideally the merged code preserves the distance of the original code, $d(\text{Merge})\geq d$ . Achieving this while simultaneously minimizing the gadget overhead is the central difficulty as usually reducing the number of ancilla qubits conflicts with achieving the distance-preserving property. This subsection collects the sufficient condition we design towards, and the methods we use to certify it or to certify $d(\text{Merge})$ directly. Unlike the previous subsections, nothing here refers to the structure of the mitten codes; the conditions depend only on the attached gadget and apply to any CSS data code, hence to every base-matrix shape alike.

A sufficient condition for distance preservation is that the gadget, viewed through its Tanner graph, is a sufficiently good expander [52, 77, 76, 55]. The mechanism is that the gadgets introduce no logical qubits of their own, so the distance can only drop if multiplying a logical operator of the original code by new stabilizers which are products of vertex checks over a vertex subset $T$ of the gadget lowers its weight. Such a product removes at most $|T|$ qubits from the data support while adding $|\partial_{2}T|$ ancilla qubits, where $\partial_{2}T$ is the mod- $2$ boundary of $T$ in the gadget (hyper)graph defined below. Boundaryless subsets only exchange the logical operator for an equivalent one of the original code. Hence, if $|\partial_{2}T|\geq|T|$ for every $T$ of minimal weight modulo boundaryless subsets, no such multiplication can decrease the weight, and the merged code is distance preserving. We formalize this expansion condition using the Cheeger constant, defined below for hypergraphs to cover all of our gadget constructions.

#### Definition 21 (Cheeger constant for hypergraphs).

Let $H\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{E\times V}$ be the nonzero incidence matrix of a hypergraph with vertex set $V$ and hyperedge set $E$ , where $H_{e,v}=1$ exactly when $v$ belongs to $e$ . The Cheeger constant of $H$ is

$$ h(H)\;:=\;\min_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{V}\setminus\ker H}\frac{|Hx|}{\dist(x,\ker H)}\,,\qquad\dist(x,\ker H)\;:=\;\min_{y\in\ker H}\operatorname{wt}(x+y)\,. $$

For the indicator vector $x$ of a vertex subset, $Hx$ records its mod- $2$ boundary, and $\dist(x,\ker H)$ is the size of the smallest vertex subset with that same boundary. The sufficient distance-preserving condition described above is therefore $h(H)\geq 1$ .

#### Remark 7 (Cheeger constant for Graphs).

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph on $n$ vertices with incidence matrix $H$ , then every row of $H$ has weight $2$ , so for any subgraph $S\subseteq G$ , $|e\cap S|$ is odd iff $e$ has exactly one endpoint in $S$ and $\partial_{2}S=\partial S$ is the usual edge boundary. So the Cheeger constant for the graph $G$ is:

$$ h(G)=\min_{0<|S|\leq n/2}\frac{|\partial S|}{|S|}. $$

Indeed, under Definition 21 the identity in Remark 7 holds because, for a connected graph, $\ker H=\{0,\mathbf{1}_{V}\}$ : for the indicator $x$ of $S\subseteq V$ we have $\dist(x,\ker H)=\min(|S|,\,n-|S|)$ and $\partial_{2}S=\partial_{2}(V\setminus S)$ , so every ratio is attained by a set of size at most $n/2$ , recovering the standard graph Cheeger constant $h(G)$ .

#### Theorem 5 (Cheeger inequality).

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph on $n$ vertices with Laplacian $L$ , and let $0=\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{n}$ be the eigenvalues of $L$ . Then

$$ \frac{\lambda_{2}}{2}\;\leq\;h(G). $$

#### Proof.

See [111, Thm. 2.2]. ∎

We certify the distance-preserving property with different methods for the different gadget families. For the graph surgery gadgets and the full extractors (Figure 5(a), (b) and (d)) we can certify expansion directly: for the smaller seed gadgets (e.g. $\mathbf{S}_{X}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{Z}$ of the six smallest mitten codes in Table 2) we compute the Cheeger constant exactly, and for the larger gadgets we use the spectral lower bound of Theorem 5 to certify the expansion properties of those surgery gadgets. For the parallel surgery gadgets (Figure 5(c)) we instead certify the distance of the merged code directly with the fast distance estimator sQetch (Appendix H) at every step of the construction, which is faster and therefore permits many more optimization rounds. For the extractors, direct estimation is not an option: a single extractor supports exponentially many patterns of activated and deactivated connections, each defining a different merged code, so estimating, let alone exactly computing, the distance of every merged code is intractable. Certifying the expansion of the fixed gadget once instead guarantees the distance-preserving property simultaneously for all activation patterns.

## Appendix E Parallel magic state injection

Using the group structure of the canonical logical basis (Appendix B) and the product structure of the lifted product codes, we can inject $k=|G|$ logical $\ket{\bar{T}}$ states in parallel into a block of the $\llbracket n,k,d\rrbracket$ processor code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ , through a magic factory and an ancillary lifted product code that we call the magic port. The resulting $\ket{\bar{T}}^{\otimes|G|}$ blocks can then be fed into a distillation factory based on transversal CNOTs [112, 56]. For each processor block, the magic factory consists of $|G|$ copies of a distance- $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ unrotated surface code, each prepared in a noisy $\ket{\bar{T}}$ state, and the magic port is the ancillary code $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ , where $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})$ denotes the distance- $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ repetition code viewed over $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ by replacing each $1$ in its check matrix with the identity $e\in G$ .

As shown in Figure 6, the injection consists of two steps. First, a parallel $\bar{Z}\bar{Z}$ measurement, realized by a transposed repetition-code bridge (Bridge I), switches between the surface-code stack and the magic port, moving all $|G|$ $\ket{\bar{T}}$ states into $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ . Second, a parallel $\bar{X}\bar{X}$ measurement (Bridge II) switches between the magic port and the processor mitten code, moving the $|G|$ states into the mitten processor code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ . Both switches can act on all $|G|$ logical qubits at once precisely because of the group structure of the canonical logical basis (Appendix B). Bridge I consists of $|G|$ copies of the transpose of the repetition code $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})^{T}$ with $Z$ -type checks, and it attaches to both sides in the same “transversal” way. On the surface-code side, each surface code is itself a product of two repetition codes. Pairing each of the $|G|$ surface codes with one copy of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})^{T}$ , the bridge attaches to the repetition-code factor along the orientation hosting the $\bar{Z}$ logical of that surface code, so the total connectivity is $|G|$ copies of the identity map (Figure 6). On the magic-port side, the same connectivity is most naturally described at the ring level: viewing the $|G|$ copies of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})^{T}$ collectively as a single copy of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})^{T}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , the bridge attaches to the $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})$ factor of $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ by the identity map. This realizes the parallel $\bar{Z}\bar{Z}$ measurement. The second step follows the same idea where Bridge II uses the code $B^{*}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ with $X$ -checks, it is attached along the $B$ factors of the magic port and of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ . This realizes the parallel $\bar{X}\bar{X}$ measurement. One can also view the two code-switching steps as instances of parallel surgery (Appendix D.B) in which, thanks to the matching product structures of the three codes, the surgery gadgets are simple and structured rather than obtained by randomized optimization as in Appendix D.

In the remainder of this section, we first prove in Lemma 3 that the magic port code $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ has distance $\min(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d_{B})$ . We then bound the distances of the two merged codes $\text{Merge}_{I}$ and $\text{Merge}_{II}$ , obtained by attaching Bridge I and Bridge II respectively. These bounds establish that the parallel magic state injection scheme of Figure 6 is end-to-end distance preserving (Theorem 6). Finally, we report the overhead of the scheme on the eight mitten codes for several values of $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ in Table 5.

### A Distance of the magic port code

We choose the magic factory to be $|G|$ copies of the distance- $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ unrotated surface code, which together can be viewed as a single lifted product code $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}))$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ whose check matrices are those of one surface code with each $1$ replaced by the identity $e\in G$ . Using the structure of the lifted product and of the repetition code, we now present the distance of the magic port code exactly in the following lemma:

#### Lemma 3 (Distance of the magic port code).

For $B$ as in Definition 4, let $d_{B}=d(R(B))$ . The magic port code satisfies

$$ d_{X}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))=d_{B},\qquad d_{Z}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))=d_{\mathrm{rep}}. $$

Consequently,

$$ d(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))=\min(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d_{B}). $$

#### Proof.

We first consider a nontrivial logical $X$ operator $x=(x_{1}^{T},\ldots,x_{3d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1}^{T})^{T}$ , where $x_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|}$ . Commutation with the $Z$ -checks gives

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} R(b_{0})x_{1}+R(b_{1})x_{2}+x_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+1}&=0,\\

&\ \vdots\\

$$ R(B)\sigma(x)=0\quad\text{where}\quad\sigma(x)=\begin{pmatrix}\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\mathrm{rep}}}x_{2j-1}\\[3.0pt]
\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\mathrm{rep}}}x_{2j}\end{pmatrix}. $$

We will show that $\sigma(x)\neq 0$ and is hence a non-trivial codeword of $R(B)$ . Consequently, we have

$$ \operatorname{wt}(x)\geq\operatorname{wt}(\sigma(x))\geq d_{B} $$

and hence

$$ d_{X}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))\geq d_{B}. $$

Suppose for contradiction that $\sigma(x)=0$ . We will show that this implies $x$ is a stabilizer which contradicts the assumption that $x$ is a nontrivial logical operator. We do this by multiplying $x$ by $X$ -checks until we obtain the identity.

Start with the first pair of data blocks, $(x_{1},x_{2})$ . For each nonzero entry of $x_{1}$ , add the corresponding row of block $X_{1}$ to $x$ , and do the same for $x_{2}$ using block $X_{2}$ . These row additions are equivalent to multiplying $x$ by stabilizers. From the identity blocks in Eq. (71), this adds $x_{1}$ to both $D_{1}$ and $D_{3}$ , and $x_{2}$ to both $D_{2}$ and $D_{4}$ . Thus the first pair cancels and its values are added to the second pair:

$$ \bigl((x_{1},x_{2}),(x_{3},x_{4})\bigr)\longmapsto\bigl((0,0),(x_{1}+x_{3},x_{2}+x_{4})\bigr). $$

In the second step, use the updated values $x_{1}+x_{3}$ and $x_{2}+x_{4}$ to select checks from $X_{3}$ and $X_{4}$ , respectively. This cancels $D_{3},D_{4}$ and adds those vectors to $D_{5},D_{6}$ . Repeat until only the last pair remains, always using the current values of the pair being canceled. Later steps do not change the pairs already canceled. The last pair is then

$$ \left(\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\mathrm{rep}}}x_{2j-1},\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\mathrm{rep}}}x_{2j}\right)=(0,0), $$

by the assumption $\sigma(x)=0$ . Thus all of the first $2d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ blocks are zero.

These additions also change the blocks $D_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+1},\ldots,D_{3d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1}$ . Let $x^{\prime}$ denote the resulting operator. Every added $X$ -stabilizer commutes with every $Z$ -check, so $x^{\prime}$ still satisfies the $Z$ -check equations. The first equation is

$$ R(b_{0})x^{\prime}_{1}+R(b_{1})x^{\prime}_{2}+x^{\prime}_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+1}=0. $$

Since $x^{\prime}_{1}=x^{\prime}_{2}=0$ , this forces $x^{\prime}_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+1}=0$ , including any support added to that block. Similarly, after substituting the other canceled blocks, the next equations become

$$ x^{\prime}_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+i-1}+x^{\prime}_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+i}=0,\qquad 2\leq i\leq d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1. $$

The second remaining block is zero because the first is zero, and so on through all the remaining blocks. Hence $x^{\prime}=0$ . Since we reduced $x$ to the identity by multiplying it by $X$ -stabilizers, $x$ itself is a stabilizer, contradicting it being a nontrivial logical operator.

We now turn to the $Z$ distance. Consider a nontrivial logical $Z$ operator $z=(z_{1}^{T},\ldots,z_{3d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1}^{T})^{T}$ , where $z_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|}$ . We prove that every pair $(z_{2j-1},z_{2j})$ , for $1\leq j\leq d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ , is nonzero. Commutation with the $X$ -checks gives, for $1\leq i\leq d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle z_{2i-1}+z_{2i+1}+R(b_{0})^{T}z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+i} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle z_{2i}+z_{2i+2}+R(b_{1})^{T}z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+i} \displaystyle=0. $$

Suppose, for a contradiction, that the pair $(z_{2j-1},z_{2j})=(0,0)$ for some $1\leq j\leq d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ . We will show that this allows us to use the $Z$ -stabilizers to cancel all of the other pairs leaving $z$ homologically equivalent to the identity.

If $j<d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ , the commutation equations in (78) at $i=j$ give the values of the pair $(z_{2j+1},z_{2j+2})$ immediately to the right of the zero pair:

$$ z_{2j+1}=R(b_{0})^{T}z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+j},\qquad z_{2j+2}=R(b_{1})^{T}z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+j}. $$

Add the stabilizer obtained by summing the rows of $Z_{j+1}$ corresponding to the nonzero entries of $z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+j}$ . By (72), this cancels the pair to the right:

$$ \displaystyle z_{2j+1} \displaystyle\longmapsto z_{2j+1}+R(b_{0})^{T}z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+j}=0, \displaystyle z_{2j+2} \displaystyle\longmapsto z_{2j+2}+R(b_{1})^{T}z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+j}=0. $$

All other pairs among the first $2d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ blocks are unchanged, and the commutation equations still hold. We can therefore repeat this step with the updated block values until every pair to the right is zero.

If $j>1$ , the same argument cancels pair $j-1$ using the rows of $Z_{j-1}$ corresponding to the nonzero entries of $z_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+j-1}$ . Repeating to the left with the updated block values cancels all pairs on that side. When $j=d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ , only these leftward steps are needed; when $j=1$ , only the rightward steps are needed. Thus every choice of $j$ leads to zero support on $D_{1},\ldots,D_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}}$ after adding the appropriate $Z$ -stabilizers.

The added checks also change the remaining blocks $D_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+1},\ldots,D_{3d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1}$ . Let $z^{\prime}$ be the resulting operator after adding the $Z$ -stabilizers described above. It still commutes with all $X$ -checks because we added only $Z$ -stabilizers. Substituting its zero pairs into the second check equation gives

$$ R(b_{1})^{T}z^{\prime}_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+i}=0,\qquad 1\leq i\leq d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1. $$

Since $R(b_{1})$ is invertible, every remaining block is zero. Thus $z^{\prime}=0$ , so $z$ was a product of $Z$ -stabilizers which is a contradiction. Every pair $(z_{2j-1},z_{2j})$ must therefore be nonzero. There are $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ disjoint pairs, each contributing at least one to the weight, so $\operatorname{wt}(z)\geq d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ . Hence,

$$ d_{Z}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))\geq d_{\mathrm{rep}}. $$

Combining these lower bounds with the upper bounds proves both equalities in Eq. (69), and hence $d(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))=\min(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d_{B})$ . ∎

### B Distance-preserving property of the two bridges

As illustrated in Figure 6, both merged codes $\text{Merge}_{I}$ and $\text{Merge}_{II}$ are lifted product codes. In the first step, the pre-merge system is the disjoint union $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}))\oplus\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)=\operatorname{LP}\bigl(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),\,\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})\oplus B\bigr)$ , and Bridge I amounts to appending one row to the second factor: the first merged code is

$$ \text{Merge}_{I}\;=\;\operatorname{LP}\left(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),\;\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})\oplus B\\
\eta_{I}\end{bmatrix}\right), $$

where $\eta_{I}\in\mathcal{R}^{1\times(d_{\mathrm{rep}}+2)}$ has entry $e$ in the two columns corresponding to the marked information bits of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})$ and $B$ , and zeros elsewhere. These are the hatched “classical information bits” joined by the pink arc in Figure 6. Each identity entry expands to $I_{|G|}$ , so the added row checks that matching bits in the two blocks have equal values. This exactly corresponds to Bridge I with $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ new blocks of $Z$ -checks and $d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1$ new blocks of ancilla qubits, i.e. $|G|$ copies of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})^{T}$ with $Z$ -type checks. Likewise, in the second step the pre-merge system is $\operatorname{LP}\bigl(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})\oplus A,\,B\bigr)=\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)\oplus\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ , and Bridge II appends one row $\eta_{II}$ to the first factor, coupling the columns corresponding to the marked information bits of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})$ and $A$ :

$$ \text{Merge}_{II}\;=\;\operatorname{LP}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})\oplus A\\
\eta_{II}\end{bmatrix},\;B\right), $$

contributing $2$ new blocks of $X$ -checks and $1$ new block of ancilla qubits, i.e. one copy of $B^{*}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ with $X$ -type checks.

The following lemma lower bounds the $X$ distance of $\text{Merge}_{I}$ and the $Z$ distance of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ by restricting logical operators to the original components.

#### Lemma 4 (Bounds from restriction to the component codes).

The two merged codes satisfy

$$ \displaystyle d_{X}(\text{Merge}_{I}) \displaystyle\geq\min(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d_{B}), \displaystyle d_{Z}(\text{Merge}_{II}) \displaystyle\geq\min\bigl(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d_{Z}(\operatorname{LP}(A,B))\bigr). $$

#### Proof.

Bridge I introduces only new $Z$ checks and the original $Z$ checks of the component $\operatorname{LP}$ codes are unchanged in the merged code. Therefore, the restriction of a logical $X$ operator of $\text{Merge}_{I}$ to either component is either a stabilizer or a logical operator of the original component. If either restriction is a nontrivial component logical, its weight is at least

$$ \min\bigl(d_{X}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}))),\,d_{X}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))\bigr)=\min(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d_{B}), $$

by Lemma 3. Otherwise, multiplying by the merged-code extensions of the two component stabilizers leaves an operator supported on the bridge ancillas alone. The new $Z$ -checks enforce the constraints of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})^{T}$ , whose kernel is trivial, so this remaining operator vanishes. Thus a nontrivial logical $X$ operator must have a nontrivial component restriction, proving the first bound.

The same argument with the two check types exchanged applies to Bridge II: the original component $X$ -checks are unchanged, and the new bridge $X$ -checks act on bridge ancillas through $B^{*}$ , whose binary expansion has trivial kernel. Using $d_{Z}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))=d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ gives the second bound. ∎

It remains to bound the $Z$ distance of $\text{Merge}_{I}$ and the $X$ distance of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ . The next lemma moves logical support onto one component. The lemma following it then bounds the weight of every representative of that logical class.

#### Lemma 5 (Cleaning logical support).

Every logical $X$ class of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ contains a representative $\bar{X}^{\star}$ supported only on the processor code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ . Similarly, every logical $Z$ class of $\text{Merge}_{I}$ contains a representative $\bar{Z}^{\star}$ supported only on the magic port $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ .

#### Proof.

We first prove the claim for $\text{Merge}_{II}$ . Let $\bar{X}$ be an arbitrary logical $X$ operator of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ . The first step is to remove any support this operator has on the bridge ancilla qubits. By looking at the structure of the $X$ parity-check matrix of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ , we see that one block of the bridge $X$ -checks acts on the ancillas through the invertible block $R(b_{1}^{*})$ . Multiplying by a suitable product of these checks therefore gives an equivalent logical operator $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ with no support on the bridge ancillas.

The next step is to express the restriction of $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ to the port $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ in terms of the canonical logical $X$ operators of the port. In the merged code, some port $Z$ -checks acquire support on the bridge ancillas, while the others remain unchanged. Since $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ has no support on the bridge ancillas and commutes with all these checks, its port restriction commutes with every original port $Z$ -check. Hence, the restriction of $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ to the port is either a port $X$ -stabilizer or a logical operator of the port. If it is a stabilizer, we can multiply by this port stabilizer to remove the port support entirely and obtain an equivalent logical representative supported only on $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ .

Otherwise, by Theorem 4, the magic port $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ has a canonical logical $X$ basis supported on the first row of its data-qubit grid, exactly where the bridge attaches. Denote these canonical port representatives by $\bar{X}^{\mathrm{port}}_{g}$ and their canonical counterparts on $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ as $\bar{X}_{g}$ . The port restriction of $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ can be expressed as

$$ \left.\bar{X}^{\prime}\right|_{\mathrm{port}}=S_{\mathrm{port}}\prod_{g\in G}\bigl(\bar{X}^{\mathrm{port}}_{g}\bigr)^{c_{g}} $$

where $S_{\mathrm{port}}$ is a port $X$ -stabilizer and the coefficients $c_{g}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ are not all zero. By the construction of the bridge, any joint operator $\bar{X}^{\mathrm{port}}_{g}\bar{X}_{g}$ can be written as the product of bridge $X$ -checks. Hence, multiplying $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ by $S_{\mathrm{port}}$ as well as the appropriate bridge $X$ -checks corresponding to all $\bar{X}^{\mathrm{port}}_{g}\bar{X}_{g}$ with $c_{g}=1$ leaves an equivalent logical operator supported only on $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ , as desired.

For $\text{Merge}_{I}$ , the same argument applies with $X$ and $Z$ exchanged, transferring support from the surface-code stack to the magic port. The full row rank of $\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}})$ allows any initial support on the bridge ancillas to be removed. Surface-code $Z$ -stabilizers and the bridge stabilizers corresponding to $\bar{Z}\bar{Z}$ measurements then cancel the surface-code restriction without adding bridge support, leaving an equivalent representative supported only on $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 6 (Weight bound after cleaning).

In the setting of Lemma 5, let $\bar{X}^{\star}$ be a nontrivial logical $X$ operator of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ supported only on $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ . Multiplying $\bar{X}^{\star}$ by $X$ stabilizers of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ cannot decrease its weight below $d(\operatorname{LP}(A,B))$ . Similarly, for a nontrivial logical $Z$ operator $\bar{Z}^{\star}$ of $\text{Merge}_{I}$ supported only on $\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)$ , multiplying by $Z$ stabilizers of $\text{Merge}_{I}$ cannot decrease its weight below $d_{Z}(\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B))=d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ .

#### Proof.

Every $X$ stabilizer of $\text{Merge}_{II}$ is a product

$$ S_{X}=S_{X}^{\operatorname{LP}(A,B)}\,S_{X}^{\mathrm{Bridge}}\,S_{X}^{\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)} $$

of stabilizers generated by the processor, bridge, and port $X$ stabilizers. We bound the weight of $\bar{X}^{\star}$ after multiplying these factors in sequence:

$$ \displaystyle\bar{X}_{1} \displaystyle=\bar{X}^{\star}S_{X}^{\operatorname{LP}(A,B)}, \displaystyle\bar{X}_{2} \displaystyle=\bar{X}_{1}S_{X}^{\mathrm{Bridge}}, \displaystyle\bar{X} \displaystyle=\bar{X}_{2}S_{X}^{\operatorname{LP}(\operatorname{Rep}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}),B)}. $$

Processor stabilizers. Since $\bar{X}^{\star}$ has no support outside the processor code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ , its commutation with the merged-code $Z$ -checks implies commutation with the processor $Z$ -checks. It cannot be a processor $X$ -stabilizer, since every such stabilizer is also a merged-code stabilizer. Thus it is a nontrivial logical $X$ operator of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ . Multiplying by processor $X$ -stabilizers preserves its logical class, so

$$ \operatorname{wt}(\bar{X}_{1})\geq d(\operatorname{LP}(A,B)). $$

Bridge stabilizers. Each bridge $X$ -check acts on one processor qubit, one port qubit, and bridge ancillas. Different bridge checks act on different processor qubits and different port qubits. Multiplying by any set of bridge checks therefore removes at most one qubit of processor support per check while adding exactly one qubit of previously empty port support per check. Hence

$$ \operatorname{wt}(\bar{X}_{2})\geq\operatorname{wt}(\bar{X}_{1}). $$

Magic port stabilizers. Group the port qubit blocks $D_{1},\ldots,D_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}}$ into grid rows, with row $i$ consisting of $(D_{2i-1},D_{2i})$ . The port support of $\bar{X}_{2}$ lies entirely in the first such row; denote it by $v\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2|G|}$ . From Eq. (71), the check block $X_{2i-1}$ has identity blocks on $D_{2i-1}$ and $D_{2i+1}$ , while $X_{2i}$ has identity blocks on $D_{2i}$ and $D_{2i+2}$ , with no other support on these grid qubits. Thus, for $1\leq i<d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ , selecting checks from the pair $(X_{2i-1},X_{2i})$ adds the same vector $s_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2|G|}$ to grid rows $i$ and $i+1$ . The identity blocks ensure that the affected coordinates in the two rows match. The blocks involving $R(b_{0})^{T}$ and $R(b_{1})^{T}$ act only on the remaining port qubits.

Since $s_{i}$ is added to both rows $i$ and $i+1$ , its contribution to the sum of all grid rows is $s_{i}+s_{i}=0$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ . Thus any product of port $X$ -checks preserves this sum, whose initial value is $v$ . Writing $u_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2|G|}$ for grid row $i$ of the final operator $\bar{X}$ , we obtain

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{d_{\mathrm{rep}}}u_{i}=v. $$

Consequently,

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{d_{\mathrm{rep}}}\operatorname{wt}(u_{i})\geq\operatorname{wt}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d_{\mathrm{rep}}}u_{i}\right)=\operatorname{wt}(v). $$

Port stabilizers leave the processor and bridge support unchanged. Within the port, the row-sum argument shows that the weight on $D_{1},\ldots,D_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}}$ cannot decrease. The remaining port qubits $D_{2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+1},\ldots,D_{3d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1}$ carry no support in $\bar{X}_{2}$ , so any support introduced there can only increase the weight. Therefore $\operatorname{wt}(\bar{X})\geq\operatorname{wt}(\bar{X}_{2})$ . Combining the three steps gives

$$ \operatorname{wt}(\bar{X})\geq\operatorname{wt}(\bar{X}_{2})\geq\operatorname{wt}(\bar{X}_{1})\geq d(\operatorname{LP}(A,B)). $$

For $\text{Merge}_{I}$ , the same argument applies with the two check types exchanged. Start with $\bar{Z}^{\star}$ on the port. By Lemma 3, its weight is bounded below by $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ . Then follow the same line of reasoning where we multiply first by port $Z$ stabilizers, then by bridge $Z$ stabilizers, and finally by surface code $Z$ stabilizers. Each bridge check adds a distinct qubit in the attaching column of the previously empty surface code grid. And surface code $Z$ stabilizers preserve the same sum over columns, so the same weight inequality applies. ∎

With these lemmas, we can now prove the main theorem of this section:

#### Theorem 6 (End-to-end preservation of code distance).

The parallel magic state injection scheme illustrated in Figure 6 preserves code distance, with

$$ \min(d(\text{Merge}_{I}),d(\text{Merge}_{II}))\geq\min(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d(\operatorname{LP}(A,B))). $$

The surface-code stack, magic port, and processor code also satisfy this lower bound.

#### Proof.

Let $\delta=\min(d_{\mathrm{rep}},d(\operatorname{LP}(A,B)))$ . The surface-code stack and processor have distance at least $\delta$ by definition. The magic port does as well by Lemma 3, since $d(\operatorname{LP}(A,B))\leq d_{B}$ by Theorem 7. For the merged codes, combining the bounds of Lemmas 4 and 6 gives

$$ \min\bigl(d(\text{Merge}_{I}),d(\text{Merge}_{II})\bigr)\geq\delta. $$

∎

### C Complexity of parallel magic state injection

The total numbers of physical qubits, $X$ -checks, and $Z$ -checks involved in the parallel magic state injection are

$$ \begin{split}n_{\mathrm{ParallelMagic}}&=\Bigl(\bigl(d_{\mathrm{rep}}^{2}+(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)^{2}\bigr)+(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)+\bigl(2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)\bigr)+1+5\Bigr)\,|G|\\
&=\bigl(2d_{\mathrm{rep}}^{2}+2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+5\bigr)\,|G|,\\
\#X\text{-checks}&=\bigl(d_{\mathrm{rep}}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)+2(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)+2+2\bigr)\,|G|=\bigl(d_{\mathrm{rep}}^{2}+d_{\mathrm{rep}}+2\bigr)\,|G|,\\
\#Z\text{-checks}&=\bigl(d_{\mathrm{rep}}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)+d_{\mathrm{rep}}+d_{\mathrm{rep}}+2\bigr)\,|G|=\bigl(d_{\mathrm{rep}}^{2}+d_{\mathrm{rep}}+2\bigr)\,|G|,\end{split} $$

where the successive terms of the qubit count are the surface-code stack, Bridge I, the magic port, Bridge II, and the mitten code. Per $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ -block count, the surface-code stack contributes $d_{\mathrm{rep}}(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)$ blocks of each check type, the magic port $2(d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)$ $X$ -check and $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ $Z$ -check blocks, Bridge I contributes $d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1$ ancilla and $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ $Z$ -check blocks, Bridge II contributes $1$ ancilla and $2$ $X$ -check blocks, and the mitten code $2$ blocks of each check type (Figure 6). As a consistency check, $n_{\mathrm{ParallelMagic}}-\#X\text{-checks}-\#Z\text{-checks}=|G|$ , matching the fact that, with both bridges attached, the full system carries exactly the $|G|$ injected logical qubits. Note that the space cost is dominated by the magic factory itself: the surface codes account for the leading $\bigl(2d_{\mathrm{rep}}^{2}-2d_{\mathrm{rep}}+1\bigr)|G|$ qubits. The remainder consists of the magic port with $(3d_{\mathrm{rep}}-1)|G|$ qubits and the two bridges which cost only $d_{\mathrm{rep}}|G|$ ancilla qubits, which is below $18\%$ of the total for $d_{\mathrm{rep}}=11$ or higher. ## Appendix F A qLDPC processor discovery pipeline

As illustrated in Fig. 3, we present a discovery pipeline for qLDPC processors supporting all three quantum instruction sets ( $\mathcal{I}_{B}$ , $\mathcal{I}_{H}$ , and $\mathcal{I}_{F}$ ) based on general lifted product codes. Its inputs are the specific properties required for a fault-tolerant qLDPC processor, effectively the target values for the three processor parameters of Definition 3, namely the target processing capacity, throughput, and cycle time, together with a physical hardware budget. The outputs of the qLDPC processor pipeline are concrete processor codes with low-weight addressable logical bases, and their gadgets realizing the instruction sets ( $\mathcal{I}_{B}$ , $\mathcal{I}_{H}$ , $\mathcal{I}_{F}$ ) with atom movements and qubit layout matched to the target atom-array or superconducting devices. Because each requirement enters as an adjustable input rather than being fixed in advance, the same pipeline can be re-run to design processors for different platforms or computational tasks.

The pipeline starts from the code family that the processor is built upon. The shape of the two base matrices $A$ and $B$ sets a floor on the encoding rate by itself, so fixing the shape guarantees a rate floor before any code is built: as in Eq. (30), for $A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ and $B\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}$ , the rate of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ satisfies

$$ \frac{k}{n}\geq\frac{(c_{1}-r_{1})(c_{2}-r_{2})}{r_{1}r_{2}+c_{1}c_{2}}, $$

and once the shape is fixed, the block size $n=(r_{1}r_{2}+c_{1}c_{2})|G|$ depends only on the group order $|G|$ . The $1\times 2$ shape we use most often for mitten codes guarantees a rate of at least $20\%$ .

Simulating a full memory experiment for every candidate is too slow; therefore, the pipeline filters codes by their check weight, code distance, and circuit-level distance, and keeps only the survivors. The cheapest test is the check weight, which we read straight off the base matrices. The code distance is one of the most important parameters we filter on. As proved in Theorem 7, under the square-invertibility condition of Definition 16, the distance of a quantum code is upper bounded by the distances of its classical base codes, so we can discard weak candidates before ever constructing the quantum code (Appendix G). To be more specific, we first check the square-invertibility condition, and only preserve those satisfying it; then we consider the classical distance bounds based on the pattern of the classical codes $A$ and $B$ . For example, when $G$ is abelian, we can use distance bounds for classical QC-LDPC codes (Appendix G), such as Theorems 9 and 10, as filters. When $G$ is non-abelian and $r_{1}=r_{2}=1$ , we may use other distance bounds, such as the commutator-subgroup bound of Proposition 4, as filters. We certify the survivors with sQetch, a fast GPU-based distance estimator developed for this purpose that runs roughly $10^{5}\times$ faster than previous quantum CSS code distance estimators (Appendix H). Finally, we account for errors that spread through the syndrome-extraction circuit itself. Only codes that clear all three tests reach a full memory-experiment simulation with our telescoping decoder.

A high-rate code is more useful as a processor if each of its logical qubits can be addressed individually with a low-weight operator, which is a prerequisite for all three instruction sets ( $\mathcal{I}_{B},\mathcal{I}_{H},\mathcal{I}_{F}$ ) to be efficient. This is in general difficult for high-rate processors as the supports of the logical representatives overlap with each other. We enforce this in the third step of the pipeline by keeping only codes whose base matrices satisfy the square-invertibility condition (Definition 16), which guarantees a group-structured canonical logical basis (Appendix B). Every processor the pipeline returns therefore has individually addressable logical operators by construction. From this basis we assemble the logical machinery, namely the reusable surgery gadgets of $\mathcal{I}_{B}$ , the high-rate surgery and parallel magic-state injection of $\mathcal{I}_{H}$ , and the full extractor of $\mathcal{I}_{F}$ (Appendix D and Appendix E), turning the memory into a universal fault-tolerant processor. We establish the fault tolerance of these gadgets with theoretical proofs and benchmark them with the telescoping decoder.

The final stage of the pipeline matches each surviving code to its target hardware. On atom arrays, the pipeline optimizes the placement, labeling, and movement of the atoms based on the group and product structure of the mitten codes. We optimize and benchmark the cost for both atom-array and superconducting layouts; this stage fixes the cycle time of the resulting quantum processors (Appendix J). Validation at any stage can feed back to the earlier ones, as shown by the dashed arrows in Fig. 3, so a design that misses a distance, decoding, or hardware target—such as a shortfall in processing capacity, throughput, or cycle time—is retuned by changing the group, the base matrices, or the schedule.
